quote: we came to Camp Creek where the first real sight of what we might expect on a larger scale met our view, about 20 California Waggons all encamped on the creek... a number of men busy constructing a Bridge.
full_entry: last night was very cold with a heavy frost. we made an early start and crossed the creek Belly deep. then over a fine prairie to a log cabNin were we met an old Tergme- gant who had Corn for Sale at 207 per Bus. had to buy 15 Bus. Couldn't steal Eggs As usual she kept 4 strict watch, Soon arrived at the Father of Waters, swo lt to his utmost neight. cane to Pointasoouc & then 4 miles down the river to some name I don't mind opposite to Fort Madi- son where we seen about 30 waggons like ourselves all bound for the gold regions and as the Boat only crossed 5 times Each day we had to wait untill almost dark however after considerable trouble we all crossed safe and en- camped at the lower end of town.

quote: We arrived at the Kansas River and crossed at a good Ferry established by the government, the water was about 250 yds wide; we ferried the wagon & Swam the cattle.
full_entry: We arrived at the Kansas River and crossed at a good Ferry established by the government, the water was about 250 yds wide; we ferried the wagon & Swam the cattle cost each wagon about one & quarter doll, and continued about 3 miles to a fine prairie where we camped at an Indian Settle- ment of good Houses and Farms the man near whose House we slept was a regular Caurch memoer and his Children attended School, 20 m. Bowers - Back Jack Grove -

quote: at night we encamped in Black Jack Grove - if a few stunted Trees can be called a grove. 18 miles.
full_entry: We now reached the large and Boundless prairie the vision strained in vain for Timber with the exception of a few Scattered Trees on small runs we now began really for the first time to be aware that we were in the Indian Terri- tory, immense plains extended on all sides everything de- noted that we were now approaching the country of the Indian, the Buffalo, the elk etc as numerous herds of the last were passed near the Road. previous to our leaving the Road lead- ing to. the South Pass hundreds of Wagons were on every side of us but when we struck into the Santa Fe trail tae number considerably diminished still hundregds were on the Road. to try and form the least Idea of the multitudes bound on this gold digging excursion would be utterly impossible. Some times a train of one or Two hundred Mules with Pack, saddles, Boxes, Sales and all the parAphranalia of an outrfit would pass us. onwards a loaded mule would run then Stop eat a mouthful of Grass untile one of the drivers came up when the Grack of his whip whould once more make him move forward. it Kept up a continued excitement. Mexicans Ind- ians,half Breeds, Negroes,W/hites etc made up 4 wost motley assembly - taken into consideration, hundreds of loaded wagon, “ight to Sixteen oxen each. Surely never man expected to see Such Sights in an Indian Country - Every fellow armed to the Teeth “iffle,Pistols Bowie Kaives,Dirks etc ornamented his Body jon ais head a large slouch Hat, his Beard etc as long as nis Bowie Knife all combined to render the day a memorable one. at night we encamped in Black Jack Grove - if a few stunted Trees can be called a grove. 18 miles.

quote: We sent forward three of our men to see Mr. Kirker and Company and make arrangements for our future progress. (Scouts sent ahead to Council Grove while the main party continued behind.)
full_entry: Saturday Morning Black Jack. Grove. we remained here all day owing to the Illness of Joan Bowers who continued worse - We sent forward three of our men to see Mr. Kirker and Company and make arrangements for our future progress. the day was story & lowring - done some washing etc.

quote: towards noon cross 110 mile Creek or Osage River it was Glear and but a small stream to what we had expected.
full_entry: day Showry & cool, saw four Indians two large Indian ; trails crossed over our camping ground they approached from . . the West & North. the day was cool our view very extended. : during the day we passed three new graves of the emigrants to- wards noon cross 110 mile Greek or Osage River it was Glear and but a small stream to what we had expected. at evening we camp'd on another Creek much larger on a fine slo&ping prairie. the creek was well timbered, heavy rain during the night Creek call'd Bridge Creek, We had some good singing round our Camp fire and retired in rather better humor than our ’ versatile leader generally indulged in,as nis Eccentricities in most cases are anything but amusing. during the day we passed immense numbers of Skeletons of Dead Oxen government having about one thousand Froge to death here last winter Some places thirty would lfe in one pile. passed two encampe- ments of emigrants of about one hundred men each taey were ‘ looking after stray'd oxen - 20 miles. 25 day cool and roads somewhat heavy after last nighis heavy rain. Country Hilly & Streams plenty. Strawberries now getting ripe and on tne banks of Streams plenty. Oactus numerous on the Sand Stone Hills. 25 miles.

quote: Friday Morning within one & half mile of Council Grove... Capt Kirker was encamp'd here with his company of about Forty men, we will organize Tomorrow or next day.
today_note: Council Grove, KS is a National Historic Landmark district — the Hays House, Kaw Mission, and the actual Santa Fe Trail ruts at nearby Council Grove Prairie are preserved and open to visit.
full_entry: Friday Morning within one & half mile of Council Grove. : after a cloudy cold morning the day began to clear up. Some Indians Came into camp & I learned there was an Indian Village of Kaws within 14 miles of our Encampment - off three of us : started and in a Short time we met Six warriors on the trail they made signs to disuade us from Visiting them but I was de- ‘ termined to see all that was to be seen and passed by those Braves & soon met a small boy I presented him witha piece of Bread & ten cent piece + found I had made a friend. we soon / entered the VillXage and were saluted by mongrel puppy Whelp & Hound & cur of low degree in thousands. Nep looked on them with perfect contempt. Tne naked Children ran and hid, in fact we put the whole Vill&ge in Commotion. I entered one of their double Wigwams it had two fires and I think two families at each fire. the men were sitting nearly naked round the fires. the women busy swing cooking or nursing. One of the Women held up her Papoosie for me to admire I certainly ad- mired the Board it was tied to and I suppose the mother thouzht that it was the little red Skin which pleased me. the Cradle or Board was beautifully painted and ornamented and roynd the little saviyes head was about one hundred small Hawk Belle which made a Continued Yingling. I presented it with a pair of small socks, and after that I certainly stood high in the mothers estimation at least. they appeared well fed but were most perservering Beggars. their Wigwams were good mostly Fifty feet long and about twenty Wide - Eight or Nine feet high in the center. made of bark & poles but Sug iokently strong to resist any storm I traded for some Moccasons I gave them musicK in the shape of a Jews Harp which pleased them much, I could not trade for a Horse altho they had plenty of them. A Warrior had died the day before and they Burxied him with all ais finery and shot nis horse at the Grave; a Beautiful Cream colored one, I would have been glad to have obtained him but bis relatives thought he would need him in the beautiful hunting Grounds appropriated to good Indians - Gapt Kirker was encamp'd nere with his company of about Forty men , we will organize Tomorrow or next day - this day was Sept dry for a Wonder ~ 134 miles to G. Grove,

quote: this evening Capt Phillips came into camp, his wagon with a company of fourteen being in the rear... day fine - camp'd near Diamond Spring 20 m.
full_entry: Started on our Way to Bents Fort about Twenty Eight wagons of us got off early had breakfast before sun rise. before long our train amounted to ugOwards of Forty wagons. not yet organized. Shortly after leaving Council Grove we discovered Five Antelopes they was the first we had seen of those Grace- ful animals and their fast speed left our best horsemen far be- nind but they were wet on so many different points that they , seemed to get bewildered and one time in rounding 4 small hill I came within two hundreds yards of them, I hunted Nep on them who started after them with great vigor & no doubt he thought them Either Pork or Mutton & that ne would soon have them by the haunch but alas poor Nep soon returned much crest fallen, finding himself left so far in the rear, two were shot during - the day - this evening Capt Phillips came into camp, his wag- on with a company of fourteen being in the rear of about 15 miles-day fine - camp'd near Diamond Spring 20 m, :

quote: we then pursued our Journey to within four miles of Cottonwood Creek and camp'd on some ponds of water (no running Water) no wood.
full_entry: Morning pleasant early Start. at noon we came up with Capt, Rogers teams,about eleven o'clock & joined in with him. We have now 26 good ox teams & we organized a company by call- ing J, CG. Armstrong to the Chair & Myself Secretary - Capt Rogers was unanimously chosen for Capt of the "Ox Train Pio- neers" we then pursued our Journey to within four miles of -Gottonwood Creek and camp'd on Some ponds of water (no running : Water) no wood, but being aware of tais we had carried some along. We this day passed over a boundless Prairie, no timber in View Some three hundred pack mules passed us, generally one man to three mules. the head of one mule to the tail of another in strings of nine. it was certainly a droll sight to see the Bales,Boxes,Saddles,Saddle Bags,spades etc bobbing up & down, 25 miles. , :

quote: we had camp'd on Big Turkey Creek (if a few muddy ponds deserved the name) about 12 miles from the Little Arkansas.
full_entry: Slaughter of Sixteen head of Buffalo. one Calf was brought in- to camp by Capt Rogers alive & Well & the next morning it suck- ed one of our milk cows & was as tame as our domestic calves but having no way of bringing it along we were compelled to leave it to the tender mercies of the Wolves, & I have no doubt some few of them had a good veal Breakfast Shortly, after our departure as hundreds of the hungry sneaking rascals were just waiting to see us safe out of Riffle reach, thé poor calif I regretted much to leave it as it had become yuite tame and would follow any of us all roung the camp - but we had to leave it to it's fate we camp'd on the little Arkansafs, a very small stream at this place 14 miles,

quote: The Country lying between the little Arkansaws and Cow creek is a fine undulating Prairie, almost a plain... plenty of Water in Cow creek but little good wood.
full_entry: { find this morning that during the great hunt of yester- day numbers of the men got thrown off their horses but all were recovered,but one belonging to a Mr. Sampson, who started off with a large nerd of Buffalo, and no doubt is now Enjoying his full liberty on those Boundless prairies but when he joins a herd of mustangs with his Saddle,Bridle Holster & Pistol (if they remain on him) no doubt Be will, be elected Chief owing to his numerous weapons of defe ipe & agfession, no doubt if taken by either 2 roving band of the Gxmanchée or Pawnee with all his prépiirxna lia on him he will be a rich prize - this day the Buffalo & Antelope were very plenty but as the ardour of the first excited feeling had somewnat abated this day the slaughter was not so great. J took a hunt with Mr, Nash. we went out in the evening. he on a fine Blood Mare & IT mounted on James Hankin's mule. I-found I possessed sufficient speed but she would by no means associate with such doubtful looking company. Mr, Nash Killed a large bull the first shot he fell within a few nundred yards of where he received tne fatal Ball we then commenced and loaded our animals with the best parts, & got into camp a little after dark where considerable alarm had been spread owing to our protracted absence. a herd of about one hundred Blk were seen today, none Shot. the Country lying between the little Arkansaws and Cow creek is a fine undulat- ing Prairie, almost a plain. distance about 18 miles, plenty of Water in Cow creek but little good wood, we Jerked part of- our Buffalo meat this night... daY clear & warm, 20 miles.

quote: this day we drove 24 miles to Walnut Creek at one place we came on a bend of the Arkansas it is a large muddy stream at this place.
full_entry: Mionday Morning Early start off at 5 o'clock I stood the middle watch last night & as there had been a Buffalo Killed within half a mile of camp the previous day, such 4 concert of Wolves over the remains I never heard it was one continued yelling Fignting & howling no cessation untilz morning, as this is the hunting country of the Kaws, Pawnees & Cammanchees « they are now out hunting of Course all the Wolves are congregated in the debatable country. we had a meeting last evening & the rules read to have an advance & Rear guard during the day & no strolling from the wagons, 4 company to be detailed every day for duty Hunting de ~ this : day we drove 24 miles to Walnut Creek at one place we came on a bend of the Arkansas it is a large muddy stream at this place passed numerous Dog towns, Seen Herds of Buffalo, on the lst days sport, some of the Boys said they seen five thousands ,some ten,sowe Twenty & some Fifty Thousand, in such disparity of numbers truth might lye between. in fact they are more numerous than I had any Idea of. on yesterday morning as all our men were pretty tired they slept long, and I got up and cooked my own Breakfast it only consisted of a nice piece of Buffalo Hump & some excellent Fresh Butter — which I got from my Friend Mr, Miller, good cream for my coffee a little cheese etc, you may say a man could subsist for some time on such fare wauen all is accompanied by the purest of Air - a clear delightful atmosphere& the prospect of an exciting days chase before you. we drove to Walnut Creek distance about 24 miles and remained here all day Tues. June 5 on a/c of the Wound Mr, Barton had recd - as the Doctor thought it would not be safe to move him, & here we wrote some letters & look to Chance if our Friends in the States ever receive them. on last Friday we passed a new Grave & “letters for the States underneath, please take them along & pat into the P.O. so I think it rather problematical if our Friends will be much benefited by our correspondence. : our hunters returned towards evening naving Killed two Buffalo & loaded down with meat a number of fish were caught in the Greek today. I seen a great variety of new and beautiful

quote: we passed Pawnee Rock which only appeared distant about Five or Six Miles & we found it 14 miles, so pure & clear is the Atmosphere.
today_note: Pawnee Rock State Historic Site (KS) preserves the actual landmark and a short stretch of visible wagon-wheel swales worn into the prairie.
full_entry: 3 ofclock we started Just as it was getbing clear the morning pleasant & Just as the sun was rising we discovered Buffalo around us in all directions and an exciting chase took place With our advanced Guard ; however they did not ree turn with any Meat. the country was level and the pasture like as if crop'dad by sheep it was close & smooth, passed : numerous Dog towns, Buffalo at all times of the day in view. new & beautiful flowers Mary Gold, Pot U Lacka, Geraniums Tulips etc & along the streams Wild oats, we passed Pawnee Rock which only appeared distant about Five or Six Miles & we found it 14 miles, so pure & clear is tie Atmosphere. we nooned on Ash Greek. nothing but a few stagnant pools all tramp'd into mud by the Buffalo & the grass along the creek entirely eaten bare. at evening crossed the Pawnee Fork & camp'd, distance about 25 miles, grass not quite so good as we could wish,

quote: nooned on Soon Creek. & close to it lies the Iron work of a great number of government Wagons which was burned by the Indians last Season.
full_entry: we did not start early. morning beautiful (I was on the Guard of the Oxen) view delightful Buffalo all round us. passed through various Dog towns during the day. our route lay along the Arkansayks it is in general 400 yards wide but quite shallow = water very muddy nooned on Soon Greek - & close to it ilies the Iron work of a great number of government Wagons which was burned by the Indians last Season Tire, Hubs, Bands, etc laying all around tons of it juss for the picking up - at one of tne dog villiazes Where the earth was ecraped up we discovered a great quantity of Gold scales mix'd with it, but it was very thin & as we were vent on going where it was plentier we could not afford time to stop & wash it. Camp'd on the Bank of the Arkgnsaw the Boys all took a good bath, about 29 miles. /

quote: today I crossed the River when bathing & consequently was in Texas, about 25 miles.
full_entry: fine morning. day cool. Flowers plenty. View Extended. off before 5 o'clock, passed a poor lame mule which some train had turned loose to Shift for its seif., I think its prospect of long life very limited, the Wolves would soon make a meal of it. during the nunt of last Sunday one of the men lost a very fine mule, Saddle & Bridle, he dis- mounted to assist in skinning the Buffale & off started his mule “and never yet was found", i had a very arrow escape tnis morning when packing the tent & bed clothes back in the wagon one of the shot guns loaded with Balls went off & the Ball passed through the shoulder of my coat carrying part with it and the powder almost setting my shirt on Fire however I sustained no injury. when we camp'd on the Banks of the Arkansawéat. evening I took a good Bath to myself and after tne dusty traveXling all day felt myself much re- freshed. the river nere is about 350 yards wide and not more than Knee deep, rapid & muddy ~ distance about 25 miles today I crossed the River when bathing & consequently was in Texas, about 25 miles.

quote: pass'd a return train from Fort Laramie, loaded with Skins Furs etc.
full_entry: Saturday morning. 4 smart thunder shower. pass'd a return train from Fort Laramie, loaded with Skins Furs etc. Some of our men had letters written & sent them back to the States, I was sorry I had none ready, & felt from some suspicious circumstance that Mr. C-- had taken some of pre- vious letters out of the Post office - he may not have done so - our course still along the bank of the Arkansaw. low Bluffs on our right & the river on our left. the grass pretty much eaten down by the Buffalo. as We are now in the neighborhood of where a large number of Government troops have been defeated this spring by the Comanches & Pawnees, we travel with great caution, we double all our guards Front & Rear, Night & Gattle Guard so that we are on duty at least once every twenty four hours, Wwe have reports that the troops are now pursiiihg the Indians, for the truth we cant say - this afternoon we have passed over the most charming & pleasing green pastures, the grass is crop'd as close as a sheep pasture and all along the Bluff & for about three quarters of a mile towards the river occupied as a Prairie dog town = it must extend two miles long and more than half a mile wide. the little Dogs would bark at us as we passed, wag their little tails, set up on end (and I sup- pose) wonder at our strange appearance, it is certainly one of the most pleasing landscapes I ever saw, the Beautiful rounded Bluffs the extended rolling plain & Rapid River with its few fine cotton wood Trees and all in the very richest green smooth soft grass covered like a well Kept lawn add to all the temperature was about 76 and wherever the eye fell Beautiful & new flowers (to us) spread themselves. I picked some of the Cactus Kind Shaped like a cone, with the most beautiful pink ,blue & white flowers on them I ever Witnessed, the size of the cactus was about as large as the upper end of a middle side’ Sugar ifke & all covered round with small tubes & I suppose that a flower would come out of each : in its season, at evening we camp'd close to the river and . placed out a strong Guard. distance today about 22 miles.

quote: we passed the now deserted Fort Mann where a large number of Government wagons & other things are going to loss & decay tons of iron, chains, tire etc all laying open to the covetious.
full_entry: oxen were quite numerous & the Indians were galloping a- round in all directions, & from their continued passing backwards & forwards & signal Fires in the distance we cer- tainly looked forward to an attack during the night altho they professed friendship, yet the experienced travellers of our company doubted them for various reagons, the Sig. nal Fires, Pawnees Comanches, Kiowas, Araprahoes, & all those hostile tribes being united & in Amity made us feel that our scalps were in some danger. we placed double guards & used every precaution that exoerience would dictate. I stood on the first watch, I certainly thought on Tam OShanter when he Kept such a close leek out for "Ghaists & Witches" on the memorable night he seen‘Cutty Sark’ However I was not fevored with a sight of the Short Shirted Indians & an- other night which hed boded such direful events passed over harmlessly. .we were off before 3 o'clock & passed the Senta Fea crossings shortly after day light & camp'd in good gras¢ to reat our Wearled oxen & Sleepless men -=- about 27 miles,

quote: passed the celebrated salt marsh about 18 miles long & noon'd, drove about a miles further & camp'd on level Bottom good grass but no wood.
full_entry: off at 4 o'clock, morning fine but windy. pessed the celebrated salt marsh about 18 miles long & noon'd, drove about & miles further & camp'd on level Bottom good gress but no wood & Buffalo chins are now Seerce ~ as we are getting rather out of their principle range, all the way back from here to beyond the little Arkansas the ground is plentifully strewed with this light (& in dry weather) plea- sant fuel the Prairies are covered with their Bones hugh heads lie scattered all along the valley of this river as far as I have travelfed, todsy on the sendy & Barren y Knowls the sage or Artis &ima is beginning to assume a larger growth. formerly it has presented the appearance of"old man" such as we have in our gardens, there has been some tremendeous rains but we have been fertunate enough to be rather behind them. we can see where the plains have been covered to a great depth & large piles of stone & sand have been swept down from the ravines, Jackson's trein of Wag- ons which are about 30 miles in advance must have suffered severely, as where the road crosses any of the low bottoms we discover the Wagon ruts to a great depth. we have been moet fortunate as the weather along this part of our Rout: has been fine with sufficient Wind to Keep off the Mosqui- toes, that torment to all who visit this region in warm calm weather about 27 miles,

quote: the far Famed & far distant Rocky Mountains are now visible and our distance is little short of Two hundred Miles.
full_entry: the projecting Sluffs appeared surrounded by a lovely tran- qguil sea and some felt almost persuaded that we had crossed all the lofty & dangerous Mountains (how they could not tell) and there _lay the Pacific in all its beauty - bunt some Light breezes springing up the enchanting Scene dis- solved, during tne afternoon it was quite Hilly & in some places stoney & rough our Jaded cattle appeared to tread the road with great delicacy & no Dancing master could have todd it with more feeling & tenderness. the country is so Arid & ary that there is little or no game at least we seen but little however two young Antelope were Killed. immediately on the River bottom the grass is still good. we found some fine Black Currénts partly ripe,I caught a few small fish but the current is go very rapid “aes I found a difficulty in getting an Eady & where an BAady would be formed by a projecting Rock or a fallen tree tree it is soon filled up with sand as it is nearly as muddy as the Missouri, every where on its banks I have dis- covered fresh Indian signs. they show no desire of a near acquaintance. as those lately seen kept a very respectable distance, distance today about 20 miles. Another thunder Storm appears ready to give us a drenching tonight some of toe cattle gave out today but if we lose old ones we have had one addition. a Mr. Scofield who has two fine cows in nis team had the good fortune of fine fresh milk by one of his cows adding a nice little Heifer to his Wagon, some ten days ago, wnen seven days old it was able to walk twenty miles a day. for the first few days he carried it in toe wagon but Since that time it gambols x along without the least appearance of fatigue - 17 miles.

quote: this evening from our encampment four miles west of Bent's Fort we have a clear & distinct view of Pikes Peak.
full_entry: Exceedingly warm, the Sun Beams down with great fervoNr on this dry sandy plain and not a breath of Air. However tae View is splendid the far Famed & far distant Rocky Nountains are now visible and our distance is little short of Two hundred Miles, the river here is still rising & from the heat of the weather the mountain Snows must be melting with great rapidity. some startling rimors have reached us of 4 grand coalition of all the mountain Indian Tribes, Utaws, Apaches ete, to exterminate the dgaring intruders on their Sacred Gold Mountain if such is the case we may yet have rather a more Bloody Battle than the celebrated one of tne LOth Just this evening from our encampment four miles west of Bent’s Fort we have a slear & distinct view of Pikes Peak, We feel that we will scon visit the first stooping place on our excursion in Search of Gold as it is Capt Kirkers Idea that the Toas Mountains will afford us sufficient of the raw material wherewith to enrich ourselves. We here overtook Capt Jacksons Company who waited our arrival so that we might approach tiose sacred deposits of nature witn sufficient Force to convince those heartstrong and warlike Indians that we are the favored Race that the Great Spirit has chosen in the fulness of time to "remove the deposits” I was much pleased with an June 21 inspection of Bents Fort, it 18 about Two hundred feet long by one hundred & Fifty feet, some Fifteen feet high with two round towers of Twenty feet high It is built of Adobtae and some 16 or 18 inches thick, it 18 clean cool and plessént in such a scorching day - Mr, Bent was in St. Louis for his Fall Supolies, the Fort at vresent was only occupied by two men & Pive Women with numerous little tewney Papoosies, who were sporting on some splendid Mex- ieen Blankets, some of the rooms were neatly fitted up Maps. Books, & lounges, indeed some of the Copper colored Ladies were reclining on Buffalo Robes & Mexican Blankets in ettitudes which might have put to shame the luxurious Indolence of an Asiatic, they neatly turned a soft vittying lock on our soiled & travel worn appearance, & no doubt wondered at cur infatuation in search of Golden Hanviness when happiness wes so easy obtained, 2 fill of Roast Buffelo meat and a pipe of KenaKaneek, earth could add but little more, their pleasures were supreme, & the cup of Bliss full & running over, 12 miles, dune 22 the longest day. we still remain in the same place. as we hed an examination to make of our wagons previous to entering into the Mountains - the Battalion was called in the morning at the sound of the Bugle and a committee appointed to. examine all the wagons etc & have all put in such order as our means would allow of & take an early start Tomorrow. I once more visited the Fort & spent part of the dey in its cooling shade it is 9 delightful residence during this burning sun on those dried up plains end from the thickness of the walls it must be a warm winter dwell- ing, I fished for some time in the River close to the Fort and was quite successful, two squaws were washing Blankets and five of their little half Breeds were playing round to whome IT gave some small fieh which appeared to have a good Effect on both Mothers & offspring. I do not mean to say that they washed any faster but they pursued their work with pleasant countenances this evening as usual, here is a description which will do for the past week (how long it may continue ZT Know not) Morning clear, Calm & perfectly delightful, Noon Hot! hot! hot!! hot!!! Evening cool. Blowing & if & tremendeous storm does not smash all before / it, be certain that is within at least one Mile of you for you can see it and now the very moment I am penning this an awful storm is rushing down the opposite hilis. it is now coming on & I will write after the storm is over --~ Well the storm is over & it will deserve the name of Tor- nado Tents were prostrated, and for a Short time every thing was inundated however, it soon blows over. it was really sublime, .the fast hurrying clouds the vivid forked lightning & such deluges of Rain falling in a lateral dir- ection, the snow cap'd mountains seen through the storm all combined to render it such a Hurricane as I had never before witnessed, I find every thing which they have to dispose of at the fort exceedingly dear Iron 25¢,steel

quote: about 11 o'clock we met four return Wagons who had been to Pueblo but the fearful accounts which they had received of Warlike & Hostile disposition of the Utaws induced them to return.
full_entry: crossing those plains again I would by all means bring a yoke or two of Good Gows. our Kind Friends have in general Kept us in sufficient supply for Tea, Goffee, etc, & you see some times for more lavish use - the Grass last night was dry & scanty in consequence of which we had to strike our tents & proceed - about 11 ofclock we met four return Wagons who had been to Pueblo but the fearful accounts which they had received of Warlike & Hostile disposition of the Utaws induced them to return, the company had origionaly been composed of about one hundred & fifty men. but, the Indians had stampeded upwards of forty of their cattle which induced those few to return, the rest of tne company had tried to push their way through to California. . they gave us very discouraging hopes, Said that our scalps would decorate Utaw wigwams before Winter. it may be so, but our motto is “push ahead untill we find Gold" by those Arkansas men returning Ivrote two letters to my Dear Alicia, I hope she will receive tuem. it was a great pleasure to ‘ me bo think that I was gnee more conversing with her. Day as usual Morning pleasBat. Noon hot!hot/not. Evening windy about 9 milese

quote: we are now in the vicinity of what is called the "Wet Mountains" (& I think most appropriately) it has rained nearly all day.
full_entry: heavy rain lest evening and as we are now in the vice inity of what is called the "Wet Mountains" (& I think most appropriately) it has reined nearly all day, towards noon A heavy thunder shower was bursting over us & te avoid aeeldents (es we thought) we stop'd the Train and in that situation awaited the crisis of the storm, on it same rushing down the valley when quick as a flash of Lightning off dashed our oxen with one simultaneous bound, never did a number of mettled Racers at the Tep of the Drun, when both whip & sour are well applied, show more deter- mination to be first in the Race, Wagons were soon capgiked, oxen lying with their heels in the air, Drivers every place but where they ought to have been every one Hallowing a Stempede a Stampede the Indians are on us, I searcely Know how or by what means T found my self at 014 Bob's side holding on by his horn & bawling out my best WO! Wol! Wol!! & true to his good training he and his mate held back the Wegon & prevented his unruly comrades from distinguishing themselves ihn this tremendeous Melee, they rushed past me with a velocity for which I never could have given them credit, the noise and confusion of upwards cf 200 head of cattle with heavyly loaded wagons, it is impossible to dessribe or impagine the valley was strewed with all sorts of curiosities & rare articles intended for the Indien trade, Flour., Bacon, Beans, Bottles with med- icine & thousands of things of all Kinds the Injury was much less than Anticipated, one wheel of Dr. Rogers Wagon was smashed another wagon badly injured, some oxen much pruised & one of B, Benvards had a horn broken off and otherwise much Injured however as we were within half a : Sterile Country June 2? mile of the Pueblo ell things are now putting to rights as far as Mecheniem can effect ug ~ this Pueblo was a large trading Fort but is now deserted it is nearly one hundred & Fifty square & contains upwards of twenty or thirty good Rooms, Blacksmiths shop, Work Shop ete it ig only one story high built cf Adobes in a good & substantial manner and the Rooms neatly plastered, a large & Strong Palisad. ing remains at one and Sufficient to hold Five hundred head of Cattle it has been 4 pleasant residence, the Reoid River immediately in froht. oe fine wide bottom intersnearsed with large old cotton wood Trees and a short distance off the bold & picturesque Bluffs must make it 9 healthy summer residence as the water is almost Toy Cold, the snows are now melting & conseguently the River is booming full, we Burkied Mr. Simms on one of the Bluffs where there is a number of Graves they are composed of pure dry sand, it is a lovely but lonely spot, he will Sleep far from the friends of his youth, the greves of his Relsetives will be hundreds of Miles distant, no fond Mother will Strew his lonely resting place with the sweet flowers of affection, it will only be visited by the Wild Deer & timid Antelope, but let his Friends feel assured that all eare & attention wee paid £ him while suffering & every mark of Reanect to his conse. about 10 miles,

quote: the snowy mountains in the distance, Pikes Peak, the Wet Mountain, & the Spanish peaks all visible with the soft yet bracing Air made my watch glide peacefully past.
full_entry: last night was clear Mild & Bright, I was guard on the first watch and 2 more beautiful Night did Lover never select to serenede his Ledys love. the repid & swollen River aweeps nast with great rapidity its waters sparkling in the Glear Moonlight show like silver, and the snowy mountains in the distance, Pikes Peak, the Wet Mountain, & the Spanish peaks all visible with the soft yet bracing Air made my watch glide ceecefully past, and I had just turned into Tent & peaceful Slumber were wafting me to the Dear Ones at Home, when the startling cry of Indians/Indians!! ere erossing the River, in an instant I started to my feet grasned my Gun, & rushed out. every one ran into the corrald and in a few minutes we were formed ready to receive the Foo, none however appearing, an enquiry was made of the Guard on Watch, who reported the Indians approsch, an examination was now made when it appeared that a floating Log had caught on a stationary one and formed (in Mississippi Parlance) a Sawyer, thus we were saved another Bloody Battle -- we now left the fine Valley of the Arkansas & Beautiful Creek Fountein CaboXys, with ites fine currents & crossed a dry eandy Plain, about noon we crossed a creek & watered our dry & tired cattle and drove untill evening over a dry broken Sandy Plain, and camp'd in a small stream six miles from Greenhorn the country teday had a strange broken sterile appearance, it appears only half formed every thing looks in confusion & tumbled and tossed about. the Bluffs composed of mouldering sandy gravelly, light clayey soil. a few stunted cedars the only Tree, Cactus, Wild Sage,ete, the cnly shrubs, and the most nerfect picture of Wild desoletion in the Whole Scene I might say Cheos is come agein, nothing has a permanent appearance except the snow cap'a Mountains, we this day met a company of 125 men & about 500 horses & mules from Alabama, Tennessee, etc. bound for California, they shouted to us when pasaing that we were going the wrong way--time will tell. we feel rather doubtful ourselves if we have taken the right Road, put then accounts reach us of such immense numbers going the South Pass Routéthat we think we may still be in the right Road to Riches, 18 miles, duly 1 Sunday, Camp'd last evening in a rugged valley & Grass very scanty. drove over a oken plain abovt eight milee & pitched our tents on fhe dreon Horn creek, about one & half miles below the settlement of Green Horn . ere erossing the River, in an instant I started to my feet grasned my Gun, & rushed out. every one ran into the corrald and in a few minutes we were formed ready to receive the Foo, none however appearing, an enquiry was made of the Guard on Watch, who reported the Indians approsch, an examination was now made when it appeared that a floating Log had caught on a stationary one and formed (in Mississippi Parlance) a Sawyer, thus we were saved another Bloody Battle -- we now left the fine Valley of the Arkansas & Beautiful Creek Fountein CaboXys, with ites fine currents & crossed a dry eandy Plain, about noon we crossed a creek & watered our dry & tired cattle and drove untill evening over a dry broken Sandy Plain, and camp'd in a small stream six miles from Greenhorn the country teday had a strange broken sterile appearance, it appears only half formed every thing looks in confusion & tumbled and tossed about. the Bluffs composed of mouldering sandy gravelly, light clayey soil. a few stunted cedars the only Tree, Cactus, Wild Sage,ete, the cnly shrubs, and the most nerfect picture of Wild desoletion in the Whole Scene I might say Cheos is come agein, nothing has a permanent appearance except the snow cap'a Mountains, we this day met a company of 125 men & about 500 horses & mules from Alabama, Tennessee, etc. bound for California, they shouted to us when pasaing that we were going the wrong way--time will tell. we feel rather doubtful ourselves if we have taken the right Road, put then accounts reach us of such immense numbers going the South Pass Routéthat we think we may still be in the right Road to Riches, 18 miles, duly 1 Sunday, Camp'd last evening in a rugged valley & Grass very scanty. drove over a oken plain abovt eight milee & pitched our tents on fhe dreon Horn creek, about one & half miles below the settlement of Green Horn . Flourishes. there is ten or a dozen white men, orincipally Pennsylvannians Married to Squaws of the Sioux Netion, Strong Robust & Healthy looking women with a parcel of as

quote: pitched our tents on the Green Horn creek, about one & half miles below the settlement of Green Horn... there is ten or a dozen white men, principally Pennsylvanians Married to Squaws of the Sioux Nation.
full_entry: Hearty looking children as I ever saw, how the men strive to content themselves in this desolate Region I cannot pretend to say. probably their lovely copper colored partners possess inticing ways unknown to White Ladies, for my own, part I would not remain here if one of the Hourikxs of Pardise would condescend to share my Exile. they contrive to raise some corn by Irrigating the Land. A supply of water is carried along the side of the Hill from the creek, distance of the canal I suppose two miles. there is about fifty acres of corn, they have a very small mill turned by water, As usual in this New Mexican Country their Houses are composed of Adobes. Some dozen or so of Indian lodges are around they are a motly assemblége. there is one white woman amongst them, and her children certainly looked more pleasing to my Eye than the Mixt breed. Gustom becomes second nature so I must get used to it. The scenery is certainly striking Grand bold Bluffs from ,two to five hundred feet high all a- round covered with ced&ér ete and within four miles of our Camp the base of those tremendsous snow top't Mountains whose gorges, Valligs & plains afford a home for the Wild Utaws, the GriaSly Bear & fleet Deer & Antelope, the trees are distinctly visible & in the morning sun all] looks like a beautiful minature-Landscape an expedition is on foot for making an ascent to its summit. two days provision, a little amunition, matches etc is all that is necessary. the present intention is to remain in the Valley untild a thorough examination of the surrounding mountains is made under Gapt Kirker with about fifty or sixty men in search of this far famed & long looked for Toas Gold Mine. if we can find sufficient to hold the restless spirits of the company in check for about four months - until the fall Rains will make the earth look green & give our poor cattle once more where with to fill their hungry maws, We will then pursue our RoutéSouth, down the vally of the Gila and in that southern Region see if Kind fortune proves propitious to its voteries - 9 miles.

full_entry: that there is large Rocks of it thrown from an extinct Voleeno, some to uowards of a mile distant from where the Crater was, he will have it tried at Chideughua, should it prove rich, the quantity is inexhaustible, there is not a Chemist in the Company, so at present it cannot be thoroughly tested. 12 Onke more stampede last evening end as the Night was dark, we were uneble to get our Wild oxen back into the Cofmls, we have Spent the entire day in search of them and have recovered ell but about twenty. some of them fifteen miles on their return towards their native fields, three of the missing oxen belongs to our wagon, I feel quite uneasy about them Should they not be recovered TIT know not what will become of cur wagon, our load is heavy - T hope Tomorrow may return the Missing “it is a strange & a fearful thing" thie stemoeding an uneccount- able fear takes nossessicn of the oxen from some triffling cause when off rushes the whole herd & smash, crash, every thing that opvosee their headlong fury must give way all sense & judgement (if they ever possessed any) seems en- tirely lost. there is no obstAcle sufficient to stop their wild Career untill exhausted Nature gives way, before such imoettour exertions & the worst of the matter is that one Stampede only appears the forerunner of others for ours seems deily to improve on the first one both in speed & Fury, the Climate & scenery here are both strange & new to us, Yesterdsy the Thermom&ter was about 112 Deg. in the Shade of a well Ventilated Wagon & another in a tent gave one Degree more, this morning it was snowing on the Mountain Too & some light particles descended even as lev as our Camp. I put on ell my extra flannel. our men are now getting very fond of the Kenaheneek and at night a- round our Watch Fires every fellow sits with hie pipe in his Jaws telling some of the Miraculfis events of hia life & as I have been the only one whose mouth seemed Empty, it was considered that if I did not employ my time in the valueble emusements of smoaking I had time snough to enter- tain the assembled Gold seekers, like Schirizerade, of two evils I say choose the least, & as the Indian sub- stitute for Tobacco was both plesént & mild. I was not long in making my decision, so, now, no Deiderich Doug- henhougher sits over the sweet obiviator with greater nenchal€nee, Stampedes may go to Guines Utaws & Grizzly Bears may scalp each other,Thunder, Gusts, Tornedoes & Hurricanes mey rush through the mountaine but there I sit forgetting the world & by the world forgot--

full_entry: Started at last, got fajrly under way by 8 o'clock & drove about 15 miles to tustans Creek, the plain dry & sandy not a spear of grass & but little at our camping ground, We have a split in our company in conseyuence of a young Missourian refusing to stand Gattle Guard, the mule train with Capt Kirker refuses to continue with us. The two companies are pretty nearly equal. I think we rather out number them, I will count in a day or two. both camped almost together, last evening or last night a Beautiful Mustang - Hunting Valley - New Road July 23 severe Thunder storm blew down cur tent & wet everything. Set it up again & slept wet untilk morning. passed ® mound on the plain about four hundred feet high, .it is circular the rest of the plein has gredually in the course of ages worn eway from it as it is mostly composed of Granitic Rock & the plains are clayey It presente a striking land mark. The waters of this creek are quite muddy, day passed with- out Rein!!! 18 miles,

quote: camped on the Apishapas Creek about 15 miles plenty of fine currents & some tolerable grass day pleasant.
full_entry: over a dry arid plains no grass. Antelope in herds, The country hae an unfineshed appearance, Cheos, chaos,! All thet hes @ permanent appearance ie the jumbled up mountains with their snow cap'd tops on our right hand and in by their beres looks green & refreshing. but we have to keep out on the plains, to avoid as much 98 pessible the steep Bluffs & Ravines, we heave no road to Guide us but Keeo s resvectful. distance from the foot of the Mountains & oush forverd in a South direction, Horned Frogs, Liz- zards, Rattle enskes, etc. plenty, camped gn the Apishetes Ereek about 15 miles plenty of fine currents & some tolerable grass day pleasent.

quote: last evening we camp'd on the "Mininas" & this on the "Piquet Sir", we are now almost on the Road which leads from Bent's Fort to Toas.
full_entry: drove over an open country without almost the trace of a road & where few if any wagons had ever been before, We were travelling through a comolete "Terra Incogitie" along the base of the Mountains & in general the Road was good & as to be supposed in a country so seldom visited by man, game was abundant, during the whole day we were scarcely ever out of sight of Antelope. We saw only two wild Horses, the Cactus grew to a great height & presented great variety of Flowers, the dead stems would form the most beautiful wood for rustic gates, seets, Arbors ete ag it nresents the eppearance of the most elaborate carving & the center of the wood is hollow which would give it the most greaesful light appearance not at all inter~ fearing with its Rusticity as it would not interfesre with eny known style of Architectures, last evening we camp'd on the "Mininas" & this on the "Piquet Mir", we are now . almost on the Road which leads from Benth Fort to Toas, About 20 miles,

quote: Started early up the "Piequet Sir" Creek & followed up one of the Branches over a very hilly uneven Road.
full_entry: Started early um the "Piequet Gir" Creek & followed up one of the Branches over 9 very hilly uneven Road. early in the morning previous to coming into the Santa Fe Road, I discovered a very Beautiful Round cedér tree which on examination anpeared to shede the Graves of four Soldiers, who were Burried in this rural reeting place ahout two years ago. A more lovely plece for the reposs of the dead could not be found. on the left a large mountain reare its head & et a short distence appears like a church with part of the Steeple broke off & tumbled down, the Valley up which we wound our way abounded in flowers, some of which I gathered, I was sorry for the loss,of my orevious collection which by the carelessness of Gédfon Farrow was lost in crossing the Arkénsas, Some times to day we passed through fine Pine Groves which threw cut 9 grateful shade. at other times over rough uneven Rocks but take it all together this crossing of the Ratone Mountains was by no means so difficult as was anticipated we are now camp'd about two miles of the top & the next waters we reach will go directly to the Gulf of Mexico, No longer shall we drink of the waters which Emoty into the Mississippi Well* (*Error, we did not arrive et the waters which empty into the untill the -) We have travelled now near four months on Streems all of Which are swallowed uo in the Father of Waters, we have passed over the place today - where Kendall was taken, but we could not tell the exact place, so,conjectured it as near as nossible, on the "Ploquet Sir" Creek we seen ten graves of men who died last fall, belonging to a government train, the Velley .— Still continued July 2? particulars I did not learn, the day hee been fine it ie now a clear gold bree%e on this high mountain, & all the camp busy, Mr. Rankin, Raking, Capt Phillins cooking Venison, Oakly making mush, every fellow herd at work & I heve just pitched my tent laid down our Beds & taken up the ven. as this day & night I have neither Cattle Guard, Night Guard or any other Guard so, I will now to supper "with what Appetite I may" & this Mountain air cer- : tainly leave us with only one desire & that is to have a sufficiency as to the quality we are not overly fastid- fous, our corrdl ig in e Dog Town & one of the holes is at the end of our Wagon, the little tennants are teo much afraid to show their faces about 15 miles,

full_entry: last neat froze pretty Keen, but the morning was Clear & pleasént, Still, overcoats were in demand all the forenoon, pasned along the Base of the Mountain within from two to four miles over @ level plain covered with the richest & smoothest short fine Gress 4 most brillient green. Showing thet heavy rains mést shortly heve pre- eaeded us, it would undoudtedly make the most delightful sheep pasturage in the world the vaity appeared from ten to fifteen miles wide & all presented an undulating Green Velvety Lawn, Antelone & Hares were numerous the last efforded much sport to the Dogs but were much toofleet for . them. it would take a good Grayhound to catch them, they bound slong with much grace & Agility, this is a lovely valley bounded on the right by rocky mountains & the left with precipitous Hills, the whole plain is strewed with Buffalo bones but from the appearance of the Heads I should suppose they have deserted it for the last six or Hight years camned on the RicNlamehs a smal] stream 18 miles. quote: Nooned on a branch of the Semmerone a fine clear creek & pursued our Route until evening.
full_entry: night bright & cool & day a delightful clear soft sunshine, through this magnificent velley the snow mountains show oscasionally te our right through the first renge of mountains, the left round slosping Hills quite green, Nooned on a branch of the Semmerone a fing clear creek & pureued our Routeuntil\ evening when we came in sight of a lerge Drove of cattle pacturing supposed that some other trein was ahead of us. But on a closer approech we soon discovered from the Herdsmen on their mules that they were Mexicans, this was the first sight of them & it by no means prepossessed me in favor of their Nation, they were a dirty set of small insignifi- sent looking mean wretches with still meener looking Mules & Horses (if that were possible) one of the young men who looked somewhet more Indian than the rest had what appeared a most uncommon bulky rough looking Bear Skin Cap which I step't forward to examine but discovered it was hie natural covering & shedding apert with my hend at onee geen that it was well tenanted. My curiosity went no further in the examination. there is e Pueblo ebsut two miles sbove our camo where some few Americans & this splendid specimen of the Mexican Nation reside T had no curiosity to vieit it. the young mans Head nut a complete stop to my further investigations, I could not helo sey- ing what a magnificent Valley for such Inhabitants, Taos 46 about forty miles to our Right About 21 miles. Aus, 3 Morning ag usuel bright & cool. and this beautiful Valley lay in quiet repose when the mornings sun shown out, but in the distance along the base of the low Hills we discovered a large party of Horsemen, We had formed different conjectures, when three Mexicans rode up & inform ed us that they were a large Hunting party from Teos & neighborhood who hed been down on the plains Hunting Buffalo & were now returning with the fruits of their Expedition, they were certainly a motley assemblage, Spaniards, Mexicans, Indians & all the different mixtures & their dresses (if such they could be called) oresented Equally as strange an appearance a Wool Hat & plece of ea Buffalo Robe constituting the jarese of ene Whilst an- other had e Spanish Straw Sombrsro, part of a white shirt for what had once been one) large loose tnexoressibly & his heels ornamented with huge spurs. the rowels, twelve Inches in circumference & sufficient to goad an Hixapott- amus to Death, those Varigated scortsmen were equally Various in their Mounting & Housing, some were astride of Jack Asses not much heavier than the rider others on Mules & some on horses & Amcngst them were a few splendid American Horses, the Hunters must have numbered 200 & the Mules Horses ete. upwards of Five hundred the larger portion of them heavily loaded with dried Meat & Robes, their line when travelling must heve extended 3 or 4 miles. TI now visited the new Rencho a Building by the celebrated Kit Carson & a Mr. Maxwell, they have some Hole in Prairies

quote: left the Mora & in about twelve miles travel'd up a gentle ascent. got a View of "Las Vegas" the first Spanish Town lying in a beautiful Valley six miles below us.
full_entry: left the Mora & in about twelve miles travel'd up a gentle ascent. got a View of "Las Vegas" the first Spanish Town lying in a beautiful Valley six miles below us. sur- rounded by its corn, Beans & Pea fields. herds of Goats, sheep, Asses, Mules, Horses, Oxen etc. scattered over the green Valley, All presented a fine appearance with the ex- ception of the Houses, which looked like a respectdble Prairie Dog Town or like large Ant Hills flattened on the top. We camped on a level plain about one mile from the Town & close to their fenceless fields, it was a lovely evening & the unusual scene was quite interesting young Boys in the most primitive dresses were driving in their herds of Goats & sheep, generally mounted on small asses, the goats were beautifully spotted white & Black. Some of the youths showed great feats of dexterity by occasionaly varying their equestrian sports in dexterously sliding off the Donkeys back bo that of some astonished long bearded Nanny. However their stay on the latter was not generally long, but the fall was not attended with much danger, the ground was near & the grass soft, After supper about 20 of us paid the Town a visit. the moon shown clear & bright the roads level & smooth and after crossing a few water courses for Irrigation purposes, we were in the Town about 100 mud built flat roofed houses, but on a closer inspection some of them contained large lofty rooms clean & neat & the sentorettas tollerably well dressed in American Cottons, A small company of U. S. troops are here. we spent some two hours in rambling round by which time the inhabitants had retired to bed if it can be called "retiring" sleep- ing in the open street stretched down along side of their houses. many a fair Senoran resumed a half sitting atti- tude with her young little Mexican in her arms as the Gurious Americans roamed around, the sight was new & strange. the whole population of a Town (or nearly so) all stretcned out in the clear Moonlight - I supposed they were studying Astronomy. 20 miles,

place_name: Unnamed rancho/fandango stop (between Las Vegas and San Miguel, NM)
quote: I visited the Rancho adjoining and in his simple garden found good Onions, Tobacco, etc... at night a regular Fandango was got up when all the Grace & beauty of the place assembled old & young.
full_entry: rendered them to us an Interesting sight. the most simple Implements of Husbandry prevail and a general irrigation prevails in fact so much so that all the settlements in New Mexico are on the Beds of the rivers & creeks. this place has the Greek so long diverted from its channel that it is now almost nard to tell where its original Ghannel existed, I visited the Rancho adjoining and in his simple garden found goed Onions, Tobacco, etc, all in small beds & the water much higher than tae place of their growth, I then went into tne House & received the most politaattention from its fair Senora Chairs of course tuere was none to offer, but, 4 La Mexicana I threw myself down on their turned up bed & there sat with great dignity. but having no segar in my mouth I was soon presented with one & smoked it (or at least tried to) with much grace it being first lit in the fair lips of the senoretta herself who T pave no doubt long afterwards thought of the Americano who presented her little Papoose with its first Shoes, this i done as a matter of courtesy & the expressions of both Padre & hadre were of the most flattering Kind. during the Stay of the train, I often availed myself of the lounge their soft Mexican Blankets offered & there learned many of their phrases & gtudied much of their primitive & simple manners. I must say that as a people I love these unos bten= watious, pretentious & soft flowing language. we purchased some of their Taos Flour at 4% per 100 lo it is very co€rse in comparison with ours but necessity compelled us by this time we were getting low in the provision line. Sugar was 25¢ per lb, molasses 4¢ per Gal & other articles of Groceries equally dear. dry goods were at pretty reason- able rates, at night a regular Fandango was got up when all the Grace & beauty of the place assembled old & young Gray hairs & infants at the breast, toe mothers banding over their little interesting babes until they waltged round in the arms of the bold Americans, the music one Fiddle,one Guitar & singing all pretty good, at some of tne exciting parts a general yell loud & long would drown all tae obher music & the excited whirlers would spin round : with increasing energy. it was extrordinary specimen of tne poetry of motion, the Graceful movements of tne Senoras & the awkward attempts of the Americans but all passed of in good harmony,. on a table in tne corner stood wine, Wnisky & Brandy sold by two fair senorettas at the small sum of 12½¢ per Wine Glass full and this was the only tax on tne dancers,

full_entry: Commenced early & by 12 c'eleeck hed all safe acress. goode, cattle, wagons, Horses, Mules, & Goats, some of the Boys traded an old Trunk for three Milk Goats. it is an addition to the vartety cf our CavAlcade if not te its usefulness, we will load up thie afternnon & prepare for en early stert Tomorrow, Whilst I am writing in my tent on the River Bank, 3 couple of Mexicans are Bathing & swimming within a few yerde of me, they are either lovers or a loving Husbend & Wife for they discley the greatest effection & fondness for each other & mutually assist in the verioug menuvers which are neceasery te constitute gooc. bathers. their evolutions were graceful & pleasing, we purchased thres sheep which were Butchered in the most emeditious menner & afterwards their intestines afforded (as popeared) a greteful repest to their slayers, they meanly striced them between their fingers and placed them on the burning coals & in ® few minutes devoured then, those New Mexicana are fond of visiting each other. 9 cerrata has just arrived from some short distance & stopped e few yards from my tent. its contents three good look- ing young women , three shildren,an old Men & Boy & pig tied rovnd the neck by a etring underneath the carrata. a large old Mexican Trunk inside containihs 2 few chickene, Gourds, | earthenware pans, Jars ete & on too helf Dozen Blankets covered by en om hide, their seats, some fine soft Gey colored Riankets. quote: We passed two fine villages, Pulvidera & Sanitas & obtained some superior Grapes & Onions.
full_entry: Bright, cool, charming morning. a number of our Roys are net yet returned into camp es they went to Town for a farewell. Fandango & when they seme to the River side the Boat was absent without leave, where gone T knew not, without some of mischevaous spirits of the Cemp has spirited it off. they returned juet as we wore reedy to stert and had the pleasure of wadding across by way of a cooler & Washer. pagaed through numbers cf Ruins, large towns heve occupied this Valley as far as TI heave seen, Met an American Wagon drove by a Mexican, it con-- teined Six women & two children from appearence IT suppose they were going @ visiting es their faces were all plastered over with a kind of white stuff resembling white wash. I fined this ig a usual method of protecting their faces when travelling or expcsed to the weather but when going to Church or a Pendango (whieh both frequently happen on the game day) they wash it off. Some times they smear their face with a red stuff which looks like blood which gives them a most bloody & savage look but then when it is washed off the contrast ig 30 great, the sweet senore smiles on you & blandishas her irresistable & winning Lures that you at onee feel in the presence of an Angel. full_entry: grove through 3 level bottom, the greater portion of the way through deep mud & mire as it was covered with weter for Irrigating their cern fields, the corn looked well & the grass good, our cattle are in pretty fine order vessed some good Ranchos & a smell Town San Antonic, it was seid by, the Quarter Master at Socoxd that about 400 wegons he@ already passed for California, within ebouvt thirty miles of us there is ebout 100 more wegons which will be about the last of the Trains this season, our train ig now 18 wagons, some get disatisfied with our pelice repuletions, others have privete disputes in this way we have gradually diminished but some other treins have been more unfortunate they have even resorted to murder some companies- lossing two or three men since sterting, Todey we passed a number of Graves, plies of stone & 2 wooden Cross denoting the catastrophe, last year the Apaches made a descent for murder & plunder. the Mexicens showed fight & some five or six on each side were Killed, those graves designate the place of repose of the Valiant Mexicans, the neoole appear in great dread & fear of thoss dering & predatory Indians givine us to know that our scalos will adorn their wigwams, we ney but Little attention to hose Raw head & Bloody Bones Stories distencs below Soeors about 19 miles.

place_name: Rio Grande del Norte (final departure point before the Gila)

full_entry: Started before day as in seven miles we hed to leave the Rio Grande Del Nort & if I have my health & plenty of other water to drink, I hope I may never more see its muddy turbulent Red Slimy ugly stream it le true our vrosoects ahead untill we strike the Gila are none of the most promising or flattering. Sterile sandy, unknown clains or nearly so, Lie before us but then we have them . to cross & the sooner the better, we wish to teke what advantese we can of whatever ponds or weter may present themselves & for this reason started in advances of the ° other trains, we stoped in a valley emongst the Hills to Neon but could find no water nor could cur cattle obtain . one droo where we left the River ss the Benks were deep & precipitous, so we yoked up & tolled under a burning sun, It was so hot thst it actually blistered the backs of my 1849 Broken Axles —~ Ducka - Fever & Ague ~ Pege 60 Good & Bad Seot, 3 Hands, TI ynrotected my face by slouching my hat. our poor eattle crawled slong with Tongues henging out, the road was Hilly & rough & on a sidling rocky Bluff we broke our hind Axle but by great care & patching up we contrived to get into Camp sbout an hour efter dark & unyoked at a ecuple of Ponds whare the oxen made e tremend&ous rush & ‘ after some time 211 obtained sufficient to allay their thiret., one of the Ponds we kept sacred for ourselves & altho pretty hot as you mey suppose under such a sun yet we thought it delicious,by. way of Parenthesis I would say let no man buy a vagon from Spears of Peoria if he can obtain one elsewhere & if he cannot let him do without one, there was 6 of his make in our train & they ocaAssioned more éeley ten times over then ali the rest es we had to keep econtinuelly mending them - our front sxle tree broke et Green Horn = distance 20 M.

quote: the Mimbres mountains all Broken and scattered into fantastic Peaks and strange Wild forms, the immense boulders and burnt blocks of Lava.
full_entry: Arose this morning with anything but @ disposition to enjoy the beauty of the rising Sun & the splendid Landscape spread around, the Mimbres mcunteins all Broken & scattered into fantastic Peaks & strange Wild forms, the immense beuldere & burnt blocks of Lava scettered in every direction showed conclusively that fire had been the principle agent in their formation, Some of the Hills were beeutifully dotted with solitary cedars of from 12 to 25 feet high voerfectly circular & each one would have been en ornament to the most tastefully arranged Garden, the Road wound through the mountains until& evening when we obtained a charming view of sone 40 miles in a south west direction, the Hills & Vellids in the setting sun presenting a delightful Landscane ~ the forenoon had heen very hot & no water for our thirsty cattle until& about three o'clock & then e quagmire oresented itself with considerable digging we obtained a suffieclency of very muddy thick water to allay their burning thirst. the 8 oxen in our Wazon drenk upwerds of 100 Gallons ~ the Idea of hatling water over pleins for oxen is prepcsterous - the Grass since leaving the Rio Grande has been covered with a large rovgh ceteroillar looking worm from 2 to 4 inches long cf ® yellowish color we feel aoprehensive that it may make our cattle sick ~ so far no bad effects - Camoed shortly after dark without water, 20 miles,

quote: camped shortly after noon in the Rio Mimbres a clear stream, some of the other trains arrived here and camped as the water was good.
full_entry: Herly start, Roed over 2 comparative Level comosed of hard cley & send covered with Round burnt stones very severe on the Oxens feet @ round speery Kind of Cactus very Plenty with a tall straight stem in the center 15 to 20 feet high with bunches of seeds near & sround the top. it makes e good fishing pole, Whic stalk or walking cane, Various other Kinde of the Cacti species goundant =- immense morning Glories es large as & conmon saucer found today - Mejor Convolvulous — camped shortly after noon in the Rio Mimbres a clear stream, some of the other trains arrived here & camped as the water was good. the man who was stebed last Saturdsy hes since died of the wound, the murderer is still in Custcdy it is not Known yet what will be done with him. my Ague has not returned, I keep steady at the medicine & I am in Gorsequenee tne clined to pass what beauties the country may present with.. out much notice, 14 mileg. . ? this day was olessent & cocl & the Road good over a fine teble Land with tolerable grass & surrounded with mountains presenting every shape and form ever seen in the same distance but running streams none, we found cne small Stegnant Pond during the efternoon but our cattle would scarcely touch it and at evening camped on a small elevation without wood or water, a train is cemped within two miles of ue a Mr. Gully Gant. two women & some children compose part of it . distance about 24 miles. Night Travelling - Soap Suds Lake Seot. 8 the same upilend kind of Road continued, Ocassionally it wound its wey along & Round the Base of Conical Mountains & then emerging entered on the level pleins, in one place a small Orchard of Cactus presented the appearance of good sized Apple Trees planted about Equidistant, some of the Cactus have fruit which resembles the Papaw both in taste & shape, only some- what sweeter, pessed an Emigrants grave burried about a month ago - he has 9 lonely resting place in this desert Apache Country - travelled on all day but found ne weter - often & often we thought we seen it in the distance. some times deceived by the Mirage & at others by a Blue Weed which grows in the hollows. in fact so complete was the deception that even the sagacious "Nep" has galloped off with great glee hoping to lap up 2 few ; mouthfuls, but returned like many another dissapointed Dog with his "tail between his legs" we drove untiik . after dark & were only enabled to proceed by the vivid flashes of lightening which reveeling the wagon in advance enabled us toe proceed for some time, but were ultimetely compelled to unyoke our Weeried cattle & tie them to the wagon untilt the moon would show her modest face, our mess had about one quart of water, we mede it into coffee & slept without the least trouble from overcharged stomeches or the nightmare, Supposed distance 50 miles,

quote: About one O'clock we arrived at a shoal Lake, water in some places about an Inch deep, it is set down on Cooks Map as a dry lake.
full_entry: Sunday. up & off by two o'clock & the "yale cold moon" enabled us to pick our way over rather a rough spur of the Mimbres Mountains, I ascended one of them just at day light it was Isolated & from its summit I had as splendid a view as an artist could desire to paint or a lover of nature would wish to witness, T wae in ea complete Ampitheatre, Mountains surrounded me on all sides some 40 to seventy or Eighty miles off but that one grand requesite was wanting without which no Landscape can look well ~ I mean water in vain I looked in every direction, Hills nlains & broken mountains on every side. About one O'clock we arrived at a shoal Lake, water in some places about an Inch deep, it is set down on Cooks Map as a dry lake but a recent shower has caused a little red water to settle in it, which our oxen Sucked at untill TI thought they would burat. Such scampering for the muddy fluid I think has rarely been seen except on the Desert of Sahara however all got : sufficient. Grass tolerable good but this soap suds water did not annear to agree with the oxen or else ‘ being so long without water they drank too much of this - 20 miles,

I think during the day we had not ten yardsof Level Road some places the wagons were let down with Ropes at others it appeared impossible that they could be lowered without breaking & shattering every thing to pieces but by perseverance we contrived to Let them down all the most difficult places. hanging Rock = Sept. 16 in ascending we had equal trouble but by putting on as many oxen to a wagon as we could get room for them to gtand on we contrived to get over the worst of the Road by sunset or a little before and encamped on & smail run- ning stream after a most fatiguing day to our poor oxen who were nearly all lame as the Road was of burnt Lava Flint & gravel, but full of bright shining Quartz & Curystals of the most brilliant & clear appearance, Dinonds of the purest water could not nave shown brighter & the sand of the Creek is full of an article resembling Gold but which I suppose is Mica, it shines quite Bright the mountains have a few scattered trees on them resembl- ing a very thin old orchard, principally black Jack ~- We have seen no living thing today except a few wolves in the morning & two or three Ravens during the day, about 11 miles.

quote: drove to what we considered the Rio San Pedro and camped, 19 miles.
full_entry: Sunday, lest night was extremely cold, I stood the morning guard from 2 0 clock & I certainly considered we had a oremature winter, I had my double Blenket wreped around & would have become an easy & rich prize to an Apache as IT felt but Little disposition to resist an attack, the morning was bright warm & clear the distant mountains presented the most Gigantic outlines with their heavy clovds resting on them. in this magni- fying atmosphere but on a nearer approach their altitude was considerably diminished, we nooned under a large & lone cotton wood no other trees being within miles of it & even them that were on the mountain sides were atunted Black Jack Oask, a little stagnant water but so bad that our oxen would not taste it, drove to what we considered the Rio San Pefro & camped, 19 miles,

Senta Cruseans have some 5 or 600 acres enclesed with a very poor brush fence, but the portion near the town has e very fine row of large cold cotton wood trees planted closely round & interwoven with brush, it gives the Velley a beautiful cultivated look & as the town lies embosomed in its rugged Hills with ite belt of Stately Trees & well cultivated fields all intersected by a good streem the Rio Santa Cruex it can vie with any vlace IT have yet seen in Mexico the Church i's quite @ large old Gothick Building but going to decay it disoleys good taste in its architecture. the rest of the town appearance of small patches of wratnearly ripe as each house top was covered with a good crop of grass now get- ting rather yeljow, put still it was better than on the surrounding Comons as the goats, surrounded by the population of the place & @ brisk business was carried on in Love, Handkerchiefs, needles, Thread, pins, ete. etc the town ao€4 not afford any faci- lities for such shopping, not one being in the city - T hed an umbrella which appeared one of the most remark- able & comolex inventions of the age, its uses were so various, 9 walking cane, 9 shede from col & a protection . ageinst exhibited to the astonished Santa Cruzeans. In the evening passing the chapel I was attracted by the lights & entered, there stood the priest whe very politely exhibited ell the paintings & wax works the : latter were the best I had ever seen Jesus with the crown of thorns exhibited the most intense suffering with the most wonderful meekness & forbeerance. the agony inflicted by the thorns appeared beyond endurance, the blood was oozing out of every wound & a severe cut on the cheek gave @ gastly and almost death like appearance to the whole figure. the others were equally effective Jesus on the cross, the apostles, & various Sainte in all about 30 or 40 figures, all as large as life, one fine oil painting cf the Virgin & Son pleased me much, a number of young girls collected round the door & I departed, in a few minutes 4 procession igsued from the door two of the Girls carrying the sbove painting & on each side of them ‘two more young Girls carried each a lighted candle, the Priest welked immediately behind the painting and the procession closed up with some 40 or 59 more of different ages down to 8 or 10 years of age. they sang a solemn channt Gerrata - Occupations Sept. 27 to the Holy Virgin & halted at the Street Corners sc that all the vious of the town had 4 fair chence expiating their little peccadillos TI followed them round & entered the church where they continued chatnting & nraying for at least half an hour my companion & self were the only Males present, whether it is that the men have no sins to attone for or that the women wish to leave none unblotted out I cannot pretend to say, but they were the only Devotees, I left the Church previcus to the termination of the ceremonies & entered a House where I amused the inmates highly by exhibiting my wonderful umbrella & a little dutch dancing Harlequin the latter pvt them into the most uncontrollable bursts of leughter and such excess cf mirth never was witnessed when the little man wovld through up both feet & hands, arms & legs, the fun really "grew fast & furious" but if by any chance one of his little striped legs with its yellow foot got stuck behind his head then there was ne holding them, they clutched each other rolled over on the floor & got into perfect Hy¥stericks of Laughter. I was going te quit putting him through his anticks in pure merey to them, but just as I was on the point of ceasing, the Church Bell Reng cut a neal & in a moment every Senoras& was on her marrow bones & with grave face telling / “over her beads - it only continued 4 moment & all were once more anxious to witness Punch's anticks, it was time to go & so we bade them Adois, & returned to camp, as T hed the first guard untill 11 oclock, a number of greves are on the street opposite the Church Door but level with the rest of the Street a small frame is oleced around them the name of the deceased is cut on At, ege, date etc. it is about 2 inches wide & 12 inches thick, it te also placed level with the surrounding street and soon rots awey. I could trace none of earlier date than 1829, as they have eo few wheeled vehicles the grace is pretty much the same in town as on the surrounding commcns, all their wood for fuel is carried on Boroas (Jack asses), a Carrata an unsightly Kind cf ox cart with large solid wooden wheels constitute their pleasure & Business conveyance, with oxen yoked by the Horns, the whole concern is a burlesque on locomotion, the females eppear to de little so far as my opport= unity of Judging went, it consists of visiting religious processions, smoeking the cigare ete their domestic arrangements are few & not very difficult of verforming, at Sente Cruex a fine row of Peach,Pomegranet & Cotton Wood trees skirted the streem & afforded the senoras e@ grateful shade for washing, bathing, ete. they have no floors to serub or windows to wash & the adornment of the person of their children occupies but little time or attention, Nature is a Kind Mother & careful nurse & to her guardianship they are in a great measure left. in their own persone they ere neat & but little cloatifs are of the Rio Santo Cruex = a Grave Sept, 27 worn, a chemise & skirt, with the Rebosa to envelope the Head & breast, the neat shoes generally worn without stockings form pretty much the entire Dress, to this of course there are great exceptions, but the above is : the most general costume, I never saw a Bonnet or corsets worn, 5 miles.

full_entry: this morning we were early surrounded by the different venders of Fruit vegetables ete small Apples & peeches one cent each Pomepranats two cents Tomatoes (@ poor smell article) two for a cent Chickens 25¢ each Bees 1 cent each ete we made an early start & drove down the Valley of the Rio Santa Cruex it is a gocd rich seil & has been cultivated for 12 or 14 miles below the town but all is now in ruin. Ranchieras are stand. ing every few hundred yards but are now #11 Roofeless & complete desolation rfins over the whole valley, old Peach & Pomegrantte:are still flourishing round the ruins with broken boughs & fruitless branches every- thing shows that at one time this valley supoorted 4 large population all of which are either Killed by the Apaches or they have removed to @ olace of greater security. it is not more than about one month since the Apaches made a descent on the Town & drove off nearly 211 their stock. in fact they are in complete terror & dread of their old Enemies making them leave all this part of the State of Senora. it looked melen- choly to see fine old Houses with large fruit Trees planted around & every indication of 4 once flourishing place to see nothing now but the hateful Buzzards & the prowling wolf, all,all desolation - distance about 15 mi.
