place_name: San Xavier del Bac (Pima/Tohono O'odham mission village)
quote: at Evening we camped near the Indian Village of San Gabriel on a stream of good water... a great war dance was at that moment in the act of celebration.
full_entry: ugly, with only a Blanket around their loins, at Evening we camped near the Indian Villege of San Gabrie] on a stream of good water, immediately after supper some 8 or 10 of us determined to pay a visit to these Pimd Indiens as we had heard some wonderful accounts of their general Civilization & an advance in the various arts etc that refine mankind & memoves pin from the Savage. as we advanced we heard a con- tinued mming monotanous sound and soon ascertained that a great war dance was at that moment in the act of celebration. a Successful war party having just returned from the moun- tains where they had been in pursuit of the Apaches & brought in two Scalps & two prisoners, the night was clear & bright & the moon almost at the full not a cloud obscured the Horizon & every thing was in soft repose but the wild passions of those children of Nature, around a pole on which were suspended the bloody scalps were about one hundred & fifty men women & even children all in the full tide of successful dancing they were, wild & furious & for a length of time kept at a very respectdble distance, however, my curiosity got the better of my fears & I approached close to the circle, they were as closely jan@a together as it was possible for them to stand & holding each others hands they kept continually dancing round & round some time the motion was reversed I suppose to put out the twist or Snarl. one tall Chief in the center appeared to act as Tide man & as his Motions were slackened or quickened so was the Circle accelerated or retarded their costumes were as verious as their ages, sexes & Sizes, Some were exceedingly simple & I suppose adapted to the climate but would by no means answer for a more northern Latitude, One tall good figure of a Girl appeared to attract attention her dress was certainly not profuse but it was neat, taste- ful leggins well covered with beads & small Bells consti- tuted her ne&ther garments & her head adorned with an im- mense plume of Eagles Feather was her whole dress, she had a few devices painted on her Breast, She had been taken prisoner by the Apaches some time previous & was now only recovered — the two prisoners were only youths but appeared : by no means dishartened & if they had not been pointed out to me as the prisoners it is doubtful if I would have recognized them as such, they were entirely naked & had their heads closely shaved as they were going to be adopted into the tribe, the dancing still continued with great fury and I had been witnessing it upwards of two hours when I found a decided difference in the time & tone of their monotonous chant, it got into a regular wail & soon all the women were in tears the Hair of the prisoners was produced tied to a long pole when all the warriors rushed out with great fury in their looks & each armed with a knife Tomahawk etc. made a dash at the devoted Hair & I discovered that the Warrior who made the Sharpest cut & obtained the most Hair got decidely the greatest applause, they looked like a set of Deamons let loose & I would certainly have pitied any un- fortunate Apache who might have fallen into their hands at of San Gabriel Oct. 4 this time. the next Great operation was to Christanise , the two Apache prisoners which was done in quite a summery manner in fact I defy even Brother Moffet to make pro- syliteiwith greater rapidity or of more seeming sincerity - @ splendid wax figure of the Virgin Mary was brought forth from the Church & placed in the Center of the dancers the prisoners were then ordered to Kneel in front of her & after performing some rather strange ceremonies were with- out doubt pronounced true members of the true church. an ' old lady who appeared to take a deep interest in the welfare of the youths now leaped into the dancing ring and performed various extraordinary Gymnastic Gambols it is true her dress by no means impeaded her action as it consisted only in a small belt around her loins & a rather cumberous Head dress of Feathers, She danced with such vigor that the presperation fairly rolled down her fat sides & streamed in rivulets over her well rounded legs, I remained untill near morning & could discover but little diminution in the vigor of the Actors it continued in full force shouting, singing & dancing. with the noise of what fire Arms could be produced some of our company were armed & their services were in high demand. I loaded & fired at the suspended Scalps, or rather above them so that the sparks might fall on the bloody Hair it elicited shouts of Joy & applause & I was surrounded by numerous tawny warriors & dingy squaws & no doubt but if an expedition had been on foot for the complete extirpation of the Apache Nation I would have been proffered some distinguished situation but I had to tear myself away from those interesting savages least a change might come oter the Spirit of their dance & they might tear me. about 16 miles

today_note: Downtown Tucson preserves this history at the reconstructed Presidio San Agustín del Tucsón, steps from the route Forsyth's company camped near.
full_entry: are gone & a few poor Ignorant India with a few Mexicans almost as degraded & Equally as Superstitious are now the only inhabitants of what must have at one time been a populous & wealthy city. the Church with its surround- ing buildings & Garden Wall (& the wall has been thrown down or tumbled in many places) are nearly all that remains. But their religious superstitions have had one good effect the Church, paintings, Statuary Sculp- ture, Guildings etc remain in an almost perfect state of : preservation, the flowing purple silk velvet Robes of our Savior with its deep Golden Border are almost free from stain or dust, the pure white dress of the holy Virgin is like spotless snow, how those people contrive to excell our best Manglers is to me a MYstery. I counted near three hundred figures nearly all as large as life, in sculpture, stucco, Bronze, Marble etc, consisting of Jesus, Angels, Apostles, Scripture personages etc, the Paintings I did not pretend to enumerate, they were almost countless, the Domes, Ceilings & all were covered with them, the Guilding ,Marbaling etc,completely covered all the spaces between the Paintings & sculpture, the church is said to have cost about one Million of Dollars, when the labor of the Indians is taken into consideration at the low estimate in which it was valued we form some faint value of this charming & Gorgeous Church - it was shown to us by a respect&ble looking Pueblo Indian, who earried a large bunch of Keys, We gave him a small pit- tance for his Kindness which he deposited in a strong Box. I think all the donations which he will receive from travellers will be long of filling the huge rescepticle, As strangers visits to this Terra Incognits& will be like Angels - few & far between, Some of our company traded for a few of their cattle, they are a beautiful formed animal & the prices moderate about half the price such would have commanded in the States - we drove to within about two miles of Té@son. 9 miles,

quote: Visited the Town and found that a description of Santa Cruz will almost answer for Teuson Flat Roofed Houses.
full_entry: Visited the Town & found that a description of Santa Cruez will almost answer for T&fson Flat Roofed Houses, no particular part of the compass atrickly adhe&sred to in _ the direction of the Streets, an adobe Church - three Bells attached to it, a few ununiformed Soldads, a Soli- tary Cannon mounted on wheels much troubled with the Riumatism as they were all plastered round with Raw hide & I think under no provocation whatever could be induced to take up the line of march against Either the Encroaching American or Prowling Apache, we expressed our desire to purchase or trade for some of their cattle, Flour, Punkins, Quinces ete and that we would remain in their Neighborhood for two days. they informed us that their cattle should remain in the corrél next day until all were supplied, we traded off a worn down ox (Dick) & Gave four Dollars cash for which we obtained a handsome young Bull. I purchased another as a mate for him for which I paid 14% fourteen Dollars, thus our team was made up to its original number. (4:yoke) we had considerable difficulty with them but by Coéking Oct. 6 care soon broke them to Harness altho their Ana@usian Origén was fully sustained in their bold & vigorous attempts to retain their Liberty, they were the most beautiful & perfectly formed animals I ever saw, the Train gob a complete supply of those spirited creatures. some of the young Cows were as clean in the limbs as a deer & perfectly gentle in all their movements, They would have made a handsome addition to a United States farm yard, I visited the paintings ete. Kept in a Room adjoining the Church as I was anxious to avail myself of all facilities in forming a correct judgment of the Mexicans - in their Religion, Manners, customs, Paint- ings, etc, aman entered & selecting a small Bier, turned towards me & appeared pleased with the examina- tion whether it was my Patriarckxal appearance (as I had been for 6 months innocent of the inroads of a Razor) or the Superior quality of my Gun both having been duly & carefully examined I pretend not to say, probably both were prepossessing, but he invited me in the Kindest manner to accompany him, we soon entered his House where a number of fexmales were assembled around. Something which I at first supposed was a highly decorated Wax Doll but on a closer inspection discovered it to be a deceased Child of 4 or 5 years old, it was gaudily ornamented with Ribbons & Painted paper cut in various handsome devices, a small Cross placed on its breast & in each hand a flower, I sat down & with great patience waited to see what part of the ceremony I was to perform, the Priest now entered & a number of Candles being lighted the order of Procession wes formed.’ the fire Arms took the lead. that is the old fellow who had been for the Bier & self. he armed with an old Musket & I with my Double Barreld & each flanked by &@ Boy who carried powder, next the Music a Fiddle & a Guitar, next the Body & four Candle bearers (it was now dark) then the Priest & last all the mourners, chaknters, singers etc. all women, the Priest the Music & the Military being all the men present. in this order we approached the church but halted at all the street corners to give the Inhabitants a little Music, singing & firing all of which was performed with great decorum, the Body was laid down on the Altér & the fiddle & Guitar struck up a merry Waltz. the Priest & women sung & at the close of each plece we fired off our Guns. then would succeed a son chaunt & at every pause bang went our Guns, again in this manner which constituted quite a variety in the Funeral Ceremonies, we remained some hours, when thinking it full time to return to Camp I bade my companion in Arms adieu but certainly not with- out the most pressing solicitations to remain untild all was completed, ? Sunday to day we remained in Camp making preparations to resume our Journey Tomorrow, & held quite a Service being surrounded all the time with groups of men, Women, & Children, Our Train here divided only 11 wagons now rem@ining in the Company to which I belonged the reason Pima Village - Severe times Oct, 7? was that serious accounts of the Scarcity of Grass & Water on the rest of our journey let’ us to this conclusion - I visited the town & witnessed some of their culinary operations a fine fat girl sat at a small fire (out side the Door) & with her platter of dough at her side would take off small pieces about the size of an Egg flatten it between her hands & then throw it back & forward from hand to hand with great rapidity, where she soon reduced it to a thin round cake as large as a good dinner plate and as thin as a wafer. it was then flung on a hot earthen pan of circular & concave shape and iy a few seconds was cooked, it certainly required quite*quantity to stay the stomach of an hungry man, put they were produced with great expedition.

quote: after a drive of about 3 miles we came to the Gila River, that long looked for & anxiously expected place of Relief.
full_entry: after a drive of about 3 miles we came to the Gila River, that long looked for & anxiously expected place of Relief but it was a sandy barren soil covered with mezquite ete ~ Of the ari copes Indians Oct. 12 bushes with a few good cotton wood trees immediately on its bank. we unyoked & let our pairsty cattle have a hearty drink of its muddy turbul&nt waters, I took @ refreshing bath & we remained here some 5 or 4 hours surrounded by some fine looking Indians of the Maricopa tribe in fact the best specimens of the Human Race divine I ever saw either White,Black or Copper - we moved down in the evening 5 miles nearer their village. 8 miles 135 as we intended remaining at the Pimd Village some time to trade off our exhausted stock & if possible to provide some provisions for the Desert. I started off in advance of the wagons which were to follow down & encamp in front of the Chiefs residence, my path led through tangled Mezquite & low thorny shrubs untill suddenly I came to an opening containing 50 or 60 low huts, surrounded by men,women.Dogs etc, their Huts are low not more than five feet high & nearly circular rather oblong about twenty feet in diameter & flat on top made of willows & straw. in front they have generally a square flat shed about 6 feet high 12 feet square their door or entrance is 30 inches : high & 22 inches wide so of course they have to crawl in on their hands & Knees but they are very expert at it - they pop in & out like Rats in their holes, I tried the . experiment but found it a tedigus and difficult operation & the examination hardly repait me for the trouble, the inside consisted of a straw mat & a few earthen ware utensils with gourd etc the women were either busy examining each others heads, where they appeared to be reaping an abundant harvest or pounding corn, mezquite Beans, or grinding wheat at all of which occupations they appeared busy munching. an unfortunate louse met the same fate as a stray grain of wheat or a strolling Bean their dress was very primative, something wrapped around the loins : & a few beads or trinkets around the neck was the only Dress of the adults the younger portion were some of them entirely incommoded with even that much, the men were equally plain in their appes* i however, some of the Dandys sported a vest or prob€bly a shirt, but the nether extremity was entirely "Au Natural" we remained in front of his Highnesses Residence Don Antonio De Luna who with his Lady senora & his accomplished Daughter Donna Cynthia Sylvia Luna paid us a distinguished visit, his highness was dressed in a Brogory shirt,Blue pants & an old mili- tary frock coat prob&bly presented by M&ss xébney or Cooke he was without exception a noble looking man, his squaw was "Fat dark " Forty" & Cynthia the lovely Cynthia with only her loins begirt by an envious striped comforter. we received them as became their high standing by presenting valuable presents, to his highness we presented a red cap. to the senorak a piece of tobacco & to the gentle Sylvia a few choice beads & Gilt buttons. all appeared highly pleased & in return we received a few ears of roasted Corn & what I concluded was a broiled rat & of which fact I was afterwards convinced by discovering that such game were considered one of the greatest delicacies & presented their manufacters ~ customs

quote: as we intended remaining at the Pima Village some time to trade off our exhausted stock & if possible to provide some provisions for the Desert.
today_note: The Gila River Indian Community (Sacaton, AZ) descends directly from the Akimel O'odham (Pima) villages that fed and resupplied thousands of forty-niners in 1849; Casa Grande Ruins National Monument sits nearby.
full_entry: to favored visitors as we would a woodcock Rope & all. the trade continued brisk during the afternoon receiving in exchange for our Barter corn, fodder for our Oxen at the rate of 10 cents per Bundle. our articles were verious Beads, Buttons, red Flannel, Hickory shirts, Handkerchiefs etc. the Yankee Genius of sone of our Company soon discovered that a red shirt to into _longi- tudinal stripes would in this way pay the enterpriging proprietors for laying it out in lots & a retail trade was continued with much briskness untill every Pimo,Mari- copo, squaw & papoose were decorated st both Bow & Stern, Red streamers fluttering briskly in the breeée. we could scarcely trade for Horses or oxen both of which were scarce especially the former ~ their Horses were valued at about 80§,oxen 20$ in fact only one or two Horses were obtained & a few oxen exchanged by us giving boot between our worn out oxen & their fresh ones,

place_name: Gila River (wagon abandoned, pack train formed - "Carrata Succor State")
quote: it was now thought expedient by my partner to pack through to California... I packed my cloaths & a little provision & so became sole owner Driver & proprietor of the "Carrata" Succor State.
full_entry: moved down a few miles to the encampment of Mess, Porter, Grandall, Miller etc. it was now thought expedi- ent by my partner to pack through to California in company with Mr. Gordon & Mess. Angello;intended to take a Knapsack & foot it through in company with a few more pedestrians. It therefore became necessary we should divide the team, I got the wheel cattle (Bob & Bright) & the leaders (Tom & Lion) & once more razed the wagon (the Succor State) down to one pair of wheels & a bed of 4 feet long in which - I packed my cloathfs & a little provision & so became sole owner Driver & propriater of the "Carrata" Succor State. my two leaders scarcely deserved the name of oxen, they were mearly skin & bone & of course I could not depend on them for more than a few days. without a better prospect of Grass an article which I think 18 difficult to find on the Rio Gila at this season. however I had no alternative & determined to proceed as long as possible in this way & if at last I was compelled to walk why of course I would bravely face it. This occupied us until’ the evening of the

place_name: Gila River (boat built for Colorado crossing)
quote: the plan of building a Boat out of the left wagons was suggested & adopted... in the evening she was launched & about one ton weight of various articles placed in her with six or eight days provisions.
full_entry: in the evening she was launched & about one ton weight of various articles placed in her with six or Elght days provisions, we seen them off with three cheers & told them to wait at the crossing of the Rio Colorado untill we should meet them with our wagons, as Soon as wa Oct. 29 they were fairly under wath we yoked up & left this curious encampment where the beach was strewn with ali sorts of articles, Carpenters & Blacksmiths tools, Kettles, Pots & Pans, Wearing apprarl etc. when we left some 15 or 20 other wagons had arrived & all fell to & followed our example, leaving even Guns, Pistols & Ammuni- tion by the Ton. during the night we drove about 8 miles through the deepest Kind of sand & dust. 8 miles.

quote: I started over the Wilds of Sonora without arms of any Kind... here I was an unarmed wanderer alone at night on the great American Desert in the debatable land of the Coco Maricopas & the Yumahs.
full_entry: of bitter dry weed, I believe in my soul the poor creature . Knew me for he turned towards me & approached & as he had often done in the days of his Glory held forward his gentle head for me to pat & fondle I examined it carefully & then step'd round to drive him onward, but horrible! his thighs & legs were fearfully torn & lacerated. already had the merciless & hungry Wolves commenced the work of destruction & poor Tom was doomed to end his short career probAbly long before tomorrows morning. I turned & left him with a per. fect sickness of heart I truly believe I Never had felt be- fore, as long as the road gave me a view of him, I often turned round & still poor Tom was standing there gazing after my retreating figure - the Remainder of that days Journey was a most sorrowful one I could not get the thoughts of Tom out of my head, in fancy I seen the first solitary wolf steal close up to him when the shades of even- ing began to thicken & give his long peculiar whine when game or Prey can be run down. then the answering call from Hill to Hill & all over the plaine. they soon collect in hundreds, poor Tom looks round in Terror but no help is nigh, the cold sweat stands on his haggard forehead but boldly & bravely he braces his worn down frame for the deathly struggle but alas his Enemies are too numerous front, Rear sides & all are attacked at the seme minute & soon poor Tom falls & is almost instantly torn in pieces & swallowed whilst yet quivering & scarcely dead ~ The Evening began to blow cold & heavy rain descended no wagons were in . sight, I began to think it full time to look out for some protection against the storm for the night, but could find nothing better than a large & branching Mezquite Tree under whose, low branches I contrived to crawl & scrape away @ place to lye down, I then collected all the loose sticks around & made a fire, went to the nearest slough & filled my tin cup with water placed it on the fire & put my coffee into it, determined to have a strong cup by way of helping me to pass a Greary night in this lonely abode, it was soon boiled & cooled & I prepared to eat my dry Biscuit & drink my strong cup of coffee, but Oh! misery, it was perfectly salt, I having diped my cup of water from one of those salt marshes so Coniin on the Gila, Well, well, I eat my dry bread & wished for better times. I now began to think of my safety against Wolves, Indians ete of the latter I was not afraid but the former required some precaution, I cut a few long sticks & Kept one end of them still burning in the fire so that at any : time I would have 4 fine brand to fight them with, I dozed over my fire as well as the cold would permit me & by keeping Nep close I recd considerable warmth from his Hairy covering / in this way the tedious hours of the Night wore along & I was @ Kind of half asleep when a most tremendeous yell broke close beside me & some 50 or 60 wolves in full ery rushed close past, I thought I was lost, but I was not the object. Something a few yards in advanee appeared to be the devoted / victim & on they rushed untils all were past & I had time to breathe freely once more, there I stood with a fire my 4 quadrupeds Nov. 1 brand in each hand but I threw them down & placed more wood on my fire & wished for day. At last it came & a more sorrowful day or uncomfortable night I hope never again to pass. 355 miles,

place_name: Junction of the Gila and Colorado (Ferry / Yuma crossing)
quote: we started before day with the expectation of reaching the Ferry near the Junction of the Gila with the Colorado.
today_note: This is the Yuma Crossing, now Yuma Crossing National Heritage Area — the Colorado River Quartermaster Depot State Historic Park sits right at the crossing site.
full_entry: we started before day with the expectation of reach- ing the Ferry near the Junction of the Gila with the Color- ado, the day was as usual very fine & the nights cool & bright. when lying awake at night on the Rivers Bank I am often much pleased with the noise or rather musical tones . of the Beaver it resembles the cooing of the Dove but somewhat loudef, I have frequently sat for hours watching them playing & sporting in the water they splash through it like a set of school Boys taking a holiday Bathe, this River must present great attractions for the trapper as traces of the Beaver are every where to be found trees are cut down in all directions the young willows more particu-~ larly/it appears the favorite tree, towards noon we were fairly surrounded by Indians galloping & carroliffing round us on their fine little & symetrical nags, but none of which could we purchase, we now Knew that we were in the vicinity of the ferry as those Indians (The Yumahs) have a small vil- lage near the mouth of the Gila Mexicans were meeting us in numbers, I stored counted 158 Pack Horses & mules they were a curious motley assemblage returning from California whether drove off by the American Government or that their avarice was satisfied with gold I could not learn but I believe the former was the case, when we came on the Banks of the Colorado the scene was a Strange one, some one or two hundred Mexicans with a few females, their mules, Horses,Boross (Asses) Packages etc, nearly an equal number of Indians, their various dresses & some no dress at ail, the different Emigrants with their wagons & oxen & the fifty soldiers quartered here sprinkled amongst the whole rendered the Entire picture quite @ piquant dish for an Epicure painter. the costume of the female Indians would have put to Blush the best Bustled young Bell who ever graced a Ball Room it consisted of a Kind of short petticoat something like a Gunny Bag tied round the loins & over this bark pleated in such a number of foulds that both above & below this wonderful Petticoat they did not present one half the the Precious metals Nov. 7 thickness. it looked like a strange excressfince placed on @ neat pair of ped&stals & Ionic top. where the duce they obtained the fashion from I Know not as I believe not one of the whole tribe ever seen such & production as the Ladys Book or any other Book of Fashions but the Book of nature & let me say it that not the most mincing or finical walking young Lady that ever promonaded_ Broad- way or Chesnut Street could equal those Dusky Bel¥ in the Swing, ‘strut & Wriggle of this Brief & mysterious Petticoat, the day was spent in purchasing water melons, pumkins etc & making preparations for crossing on the Morrow. the width of the River at the ferry is about 200 yards & a pretty good Boat sufficiently large to carry a wagon is now at this place, it was built up the Gila by a Mr. Moore & sold to the Lieut commanding at this place "Camp Calhoun" the ferriage is 4$ for each. wagon & 50% for a footman, the Mexicans are charged 4% per mule & 5 per cent on all the amt. of Ore which is now considerable, some days as much as 50 lb or 60 lb paying duty, they have recourse to various meathods for the purpose of smuggling & avoiding the duty, but there is a serdant, an Irishman, who appears rather Keen & acute _ for the Mexicans & certainly he has found some of the ore secreated in places that but few would have thought of in- specting. all smuggled ore is liable to confiscation but in general they only take about, half,a portion of which falls to the indefatigable sergant,& if this constant stream of the pure metals continues to flow from Cali- fornja to Mexico by way of the ferry at Camp Calhoun & the Sergant retains the office of inspector general he is in a rapid Road to promotion so far as wealth is concerned = [I witnessed some pieces of pure Gold as large as seven pounds, the amount daily passing here exceeds all belief & I would be loath to state the full amount least my friends who put the most implicit confidence in my veracity might now be inclined to doubt it, but no doubt long ere this they have heard more wonderful accounts than I could com- municate to them, of which facts I am unable to Judge as it is now almost seven months since we have seen a news- paper & consequently can form no Idea of what is & transacting in the busy World - I ascended the Hill or : Rocks which here form the ramparts of the Rio Colorado they are about 100 feet high & the view was extended & beautiful, the distant Mountains presenting every out— line that it was possible for rugged, piked, precipit- uous, broken Mountains to assume, spires & domes of huge & colossal dimensions could easily be distinguished against the Glowing warm sky of one of the most serene Evenings, it was possible to immagine, ItAly itself cannot exceed in & sweet balmy atmosphere this delight- ful season on the Rio Colorado, but then the continued clouds of dust our toilsome tedious & everlasting Journey unfit us for either the beauties of nature or looking with an eye to Hither the sublime or Beautiful - quote: the wagons were all safely across by noon & Mr. Porter & self having only two Carratas we ferried them over in a small Boat.
full_entry: the morning was charming & the scene one of the most strange & picturesque I had ever Witnessed — in my possession at home were some beautiful pictures of the Crossing the Jordan but here was a living picture in- finitely more strange & picturesque - about 150 Mexicans had arrived on the other side from California with their Horses, Asses, Mules, Goats & sheep & on this side were Fumigrants with Wagons & Mules, Oxen & Horses, Indians & @ sprinkling of soldiers, the Braying of Mules & Boros Neighing of Horses, Lowing of Oxen Bleating of Goats & sheep & Yelling & Whooping of the Yumahs with the sup- pressed & sometimes loud Execrations of the Boatmen formed a rare picture both for the Eye & Ear, the naked Barren Rocks & Hills contrasted well with the deep green of the cotton wood & the soft Bright sky overhead rendered it such a morning as I shail not soon forget. the wagons were all safely across by noon & Mr. Porter & self having only two Carratas we ferried them over in a small Boat belonging to some Emmigrants & so saved 3¢# Each we drove out about three miles & camped in the old bed of the Colorado where our cattle found some little scattering Cane & under the Mezquite Trees considerable Reans,

quote: here an Immense & extended level lay before us, "the Great American Desert" bounded in the far distance by naked Rugged mountains.
full_entry: after travelling through deep sand for five miles we ascended the elevated plaing with great labor. here an Immense & extended level lay before us, "the Great American Desert" bounded in the far distance by naked Rugged mountains a fit boundery for such a sterile naked waste the only specimen of the vegetable Kingdom being the "Larrea Mexicana" from two to four feet high & but few of them, they were scattered at wide distances apart & I am not certain that I now give the right name of the shrub as I know nothing of botdény - our progress was slow as the wheels sunk deep in the sand & pebbles, at sunset we halted & fed our cattle & cooked supper & after two hours rest resumed our Journey the day was charming, 12 mi,

quote: the road from this place improved & by 9 o'clock we reached our camping ground, modestly called "Salvation Camp". 16 m.
full_entry: Mules & Horses predominating largely over the oxen - but in fact the Road all the way down the Gila, & for so far is plentifully strewn with food for buzzards, wolves & Ravens ~ the latter being the only specimen of life we have seen since ascending the Bluff, the remains of Wagons were here in plentiful profusion. when we wished to Kindle a fire for cooking purgoses a handsome Eastern built wagon frequently supplied the material, it was no unusual thing to see a Troy Built Vehicle supply the fuel for meArly warming up a little cold coffee, "to what poor uses we may come at last" in two miles further we came to a Lagoon with an abundance of Stagnant Water where all were duly refreshed but like the past well the mortality had been great & not entirely confined to the cattle as five new Graves were here, one of which was only three days before from the boards olaced at the Grave head, they all appeared to have been from Arkansas, it was evident that the last deceased had only been in Company with another man as from the place where he died he had been haWled on a few Bushes to his grave. his old clothing still remained where he died. it certainly was a gloomy picture & a dreary resting place & awful solitude must surround this muddy Lagoon when the few travellers shall cease to pass by these Golgothas ~- the road from this place improved & by 9 o clock we reached our camping ground, modestly called "Salvation Camp" 16 m

quote: in about 2 miles we found a little running water trickling down the almost dry bed of Corrigo Creek, this was the first we had seen since leaving the Colorado.
full_entry: fine morning with a few fleeting clouds & as early as the first dawn made its appearance we were off in about 2 miles we found @ little running water trickling down ‘ the almost dry bed of Corrigo Creek, this was the first we had seen since leaving the Colorado. the Bed of this Creek is between two rocky Barren mountains, not a part- icle of Gress or indeed any thing else with the exception of the Larrea Mexicana & a few other stunted shrubs ail in utter desolation. it is impossible to immagine the complete waste & sterile appearance of those peaked, Jagged, Pointed, & Hillocky mountains. the Genius of Bolitude Desolation & Death rains over all here without controle, let or hinderance once for all. at no time are you ever out of sight of Dead Mules, Horses, or Oxen & I have even seen that sight which Mr. Saml Weller con- sidered problematical - a Dead Ass, that instinctive pertinacity with which it is said they cling to life was found here unable to protect them against the desolating Angel of the Desert, so that long mooted question may now be set at rest "Asses do die" — as the morning advanced Livid Clouds began to overshadow the sun & in a short time fitful gusts of Wind rushed down between the mountains, then for a moment or two a lull would ensue, but this would be succeeded by stronger & heavier gusts whirling & dash- ing the loose sand in our Eyes & completely obstructing @ Miserable Night Nov, 22 all view in a short time so severe did the Hurricane become that we could barely proceed the sand whirled & Eddied around us filling every opening, Eyes, Ears & Mouth, all traces of the road were nearly obliterated, the oxen in their weak state stumbled siowly along & by holding on to the wagon we continued to dreg our weary limbs through this simoon of shifting sand. a few yards at a time was all we could overcome, the wind blew cold & frosty the sudden change affected us much as we were not prepared for it & we suffered much from the cold, I had faced many a storm of Rain, Snow & sleet, but such severity as this I never encountered we hed two sailors in company who had battled with many a storm around Cape Horn had suffered the biting Northern Tempests, the sudden Tornadoes of southern Latitudes, but this far, far Exceeded in real suffering any trials to which they had ever been exposed, during one of the short rests with which we had to indulge our weary oxen I seated my~ self on the skeleton of a dead mule as such seats were always in ebundance & in that short oeriod my seat was entirely covered up with the drifting sand ~ we continued our slow & toilsome way until near dark & driving as close under a Bluff as possible unyoked our almost ex- hausted cattle tied them to the wheels & gave them part of what little dry grasa remained. a fire was coaxed into existance with what few shrubs could be obtained a little Warm coffee without sugar (as that useful art- icle had for a length of time been unknown to us) & some cold cakes constituted our disconsolate supper, which . was certainly the most dreary on the whole Journey & I rather think it would be difficult to picture 4 more dreary one, surrounded by naked barren mountains, & sandy sterile plains, not a tree or shrub of any magni- tude to afford us a comfortable fire, sitting freezing over & nearly cold supper, the only warm article of it peing the sugarless coffee, but as a substitute well filled with the drifting & Eddying sand of the Great American Desert. I made my bed close to the carrata & passed a cold & almost sleepless Night, 7 miles,

Corrigo Creek, this was the first we had seen since leaving the Colorado. the Bed of this Creek is between two rocky Barren mountains, not a part- icle of Gress or indeed any thing else with the exception of the Larrea Mexicana & a few other stunted shrubs ail in utter desolation. it is impossible to immagine the complete waste & sterile appearance of those peaked, Jagged, Pointed, & Hillocky mountains. the Genius of Bolitude Desolation & Death rains over all here without controle, let or hinderance once for all. at no time are you ever out of sight of Dead Mules, Horses, or Oxen & I have even seen that sight which Mr. Saml Weller con- sidered problematical - a Dead Ass, that instinctive pertinacity with which it is said they cling to life was found here unable to protect them against the desolating Angel of the Desert, so that long mooted question may now be set at rest "Asses do die" — as the morning advanced Livid Clouds began to overshadow the sun & in a short time fitful gusts of Wind rushed down between the mountains, then for a moment or two a lull would ensue, but this would be succeeded by stronger & heavier gusts whirling & dash- ing the loose sand in our Eyes & completely obstructing @ Miserable Night Nov, 22 all view in a short time so severe did the Hurricane become that we could barely proceed the sand whirled & Eddied around us filling every opening, Eyes, Ears & Mouth, all traces of the road were nearly obliterated, the oxen in their weak state stumbled siowly along & by holding on to the wagon we continued to dreg our weary limbs through this simoon of shifting sand. a few yards at a time was all we could overcome, the wind blew cold & frosty the sudden change affected us much as we were not prepared for it & we suffered much from the cold, I had faced many a storm of Rain, Snow & sleet, but such severity as this I never encountered we hed two sailors in company who had battled with many a storm around Cape Horn had suffered the biting Northern Tempests, the sudden Tornadoes of southern Latitudes, but this far, far Exceeded in real suffering any trials to which they had ever been exposed, during one of the short rests with which we had to indulge our weary oxen I seated my~ self on the skeleton of a dead mule as such seats were always in ebundance & in that short oeriod my seat was entirely covered up with the drifting sand ~ we continued our slow & toilsome way until near dark & driving as close under a Bluff as possible unyoked our almost ex- hausted cattle tied them to the wheels & gave them part of what little dry grasa remained. a fire was coaxed into existance with what few shrubs could be obtained a little Warm coffee without sugar (as that useful art- icle had for a length of time been unknown to us) & some cold cakes constituted our disconsolate supper, which . was certainly the most dreary on the whole Journey & I rather think it would be difficult to picture 4 more dreary one, surrounded by naked barren mountains, & sandy sterile plains, not a tree or shrub of any magni- tude to afford us a comfortable fire, sitting freezing over & nearly cold supper, the only warm article of it peing the sugarless coffee, but as a substitute well filled with the drifting & Eddying sand of the Great American Desert. I made my bed close to the carrata & passed a cold & almost sleepless Night, 7 miles,

quote: a little before sunset we reached the spring of Valliceto. its situation is between two Barren mountains about 14 miles apart.
today_note: Vallecito County Park (San Diego County) has a reconstructed adobe stage station on the actual spring-fed campsite Forsyth used.
full_entry: a day about 14 pints each - every effort were had re- sourse to to make the poor exhausted Brutes proceed. the most effectual was to run up at them with the dog when if they still possess strength to resume their feet they would at once do so. near one of the Lagoons which we had past were two poor exhausted oxen & I used all my power to persuade them to rise for the purpose of driving them to water but I could not move them, at last I set Nep on them one of the poor feeble animals with great exertion resumed his feet & stumbled forward a few paces when he once more fell,to never rise again, I was sorry I had disturbed the dying creature as he fell in a worse position than I found him, a few Indian families are found at or near all those Lagoons as I conceive for the purpose of getting the exhausted Mules, horses & oxen all of which are stripped of what little flesh hard usage has left. in general those Indians look fat & Hearty as every weed or shrub appears to afford them food in some shape or other however even on those lonely Deserts their love of war and fighting appears to cling to them, at one of their shelters we found a man who had been way leid & shot in the Breast by an arrow he was not : quite dead & Mr, Crandell bound up his wound, three or four Squaws were keeping up @ wonderful wailing around him, the deed was done by the Yumas three of whoma we met returning to thelr village on the Colorado. in my Early day I had often admired the heroic & daring con- duct described by some writers respecting the patient tollsome marches made into an Enemys country by some young Chief anxious to distinguish himself & the noble bravery with which he had taken possession of some half dozen scalps. TI am now sorry to say that all the romance of the transaction has changed into detestation of their assassin like acts, but different nations have different Ideas of Glory & probAbly the Indians method of destroying his Enemy, may be as justifiable before an higher tribunal as our own more wholesale & scientific plan of sweeping them off by thousands. a little before sunset we reached the spring of Valliceto. its situation is between to Barren mountains about 14 miles apart & for a short dis- tance around has had good grass but all is now eaten off & the place resembles a Coméns, the soring is strongly impregnated with sulpher & “he ground covered with Eftlovgnee. it was rather a poor resting place but we were glad to obtain any thing in the shape of food for our cattle & a few Bitter Willows still remained on which they Browsed, 11 miles.

quote: we all got safe over & found water at a spring El Puerto (or the Door) this Valley was about two hundred feet higher than the one which we had left.
today_note: This is Box Canyon in Anza-Borrego Desert State Park — the Mormon Battalion/Cooke's Wagon Road literally chiseled a path through solid rock here in 1846-47, and the cut is still visible today just off Hwy S-2.
full_entry: it was late in the day before we gathered up our : cattle as they had strayed unsuccessfully in quest of petter boarding, the road led up between the two mountains which were in some places 5 or 6 miles apart, in about 4 miles we came to a very steep hill which we had to cross it was some 4 or 5 hundred feet high & the most abrupt which we had found on our Journey but we all got safe over & found water at a spring El Puerto (or the Door) this Preparation for Separation Nov. 24 Vally was about two hundred feet higher than the one which we had left, they are strange little secluded places, no outlet, hills or mountains all around. no running water, no trees only a few shrubs nevertheless here were a few Indian Families at this spring as were also a few at the last ~- they were now beginning to , Build their Huts as the nights were getting very cold & ice forming every night. previous to this, the shelter of the few bushes or the sand hills afforded them the only protection against the weather. we pro- ceeded on a few miles & let our cattle loose on the poorest possible Kind of poor shrubs. 7 miles,

quote: Towards noon we reached San Filipe. it contains about 50 Indian Huts which were new as their preparations for Winter were in rapid progress.
full_entry: Sunday, we were early off & our way led up a Canp the most strange & wild egress from this forlorn val. steep hills arose over our heads,naked & barren & the Wagon filled up the whole breadth between the rocks, so completely did they fit this narrow defile that both sides were frequently rubbing at the same time, it was the gry place that perfectly came up to my Ideas of a Kanyon, with much toil we gained the summit & by a gentle descent on a good road gained the next vate = here we met a large party of Mexicans who were Vamosing from California in all haste. as usual with lots of Ora - Towards noon we reached San Filipe. it contains about 50 Indian Huts which were new as their prepdrations for Winter were in rapid progress - @ round : hole is scooped out in the sand & a few sticks stuck around it meeting at top & a covering of Brush & another of sand generally constitute the Edefice. it is about 10 or 12 feet in diameter & five or six high in the center, the door or hole at which they enter about 30 inches high. it affords them shelter for one Winter & I believe that is as long as ae generality of Indians wish to provide against or prep for. like the springs lately passed, this is strongly sulphurated & an Effle@resence covers the Ground the grass adjoining is salt but further down the vally it was free from saline matter & we drove about two miles below the Village & Camped near a few 014 Cotton-Wood Trees the first we had seen for a long time. 135 m,

quote: by noon we had ascended a mountain which led us down into the far famed Vally of Warners ranch, we camped within two miles of it.
today_note: Warner Springs Ranch resort now occupies the historic Warner's Ranch adobe (California Historical Landmark), still fed by the same hot springs.
full_entry: last night was cold & Stormy, our start was an Early one the road leading up a gentle eminence, the wind was directly in our faces & the cold rain was any thing but agreeable & our long usage to heat & dust made it orobably more so than it otherwise would have been. the ascent continued more steep & by noon we had ‘ ascen@ed ee mountain which led us down into the far famed Vally of Warners ranch, we camped within two miles of it. a few of us visited the place after supper. it was mearl¥y a Willow frame house with flags for roof & sides about 50 or 60 feet long & twenty wide,some 15 feet high. however this wag a new concern the old Ranch being three miles farther north. we gained but little information as respected the digging gold, : . but he was like all the Mexicans whom& we had met, he ; said that it was impossible to go into the mines during the Winter. Here we determined to divide our Company once more the Mess, Porters & Howlet going to Los Angels & Mr, Crandle & his men & the two Miller Boys & / self ‘going to San Diego, it was with much regret I had determined to part with Dr, Porter & his Brothers, but / we all considered the sepAration best adapted to the respective wants & wishes of the parties, 16 miles,

quote: near evening we entered the fine Val of "Station Isabell" it is a most charming place, large herds of horses & cattle were quietly grazing in its rich pastures.
today_note: The Santa Ysabel Mission Asistencia (Mission Santa Ysabel) is still an active Catholic mission chapel today.
full_entry: mountains covered with snow, every thing looked dreary & bleak but in an hour or two the sun broke through the Clouds & Cheerafulness began to r&in once more as we gained the next vally. the meadow Larks were singing Joyously & everything began to have the appearance of a Spring morning. our spirits rose with the cheererfull shining sun & we forgot that we had passed a cold damp night, at noon a prowling wolf approached rather near where we sat taking our lunch & Mr. Oakley fired at him & broke his leg. "Nep" soon caught him & they had a real rough & tumble fight. the wolf came off second pest - near evening we entered the fine Val of "Sta- tion Isabell" it is a most charming place, large herds of horses & cattle were quietly grazing in its rich pastures for here the grass was tall & Green. numerous clear streams flow through one of them sufficiently Large for any modpate power, the old buildings are all going to decay the roof of the Church has fallen in, put the Bells still remain, quite a village is built around the old Ruins, Consisting of Mexicans Indians & the intermediate grades, but if the Vall was a lovely “scene of quiet repose the Village was the reverse, a quantity of the ardent had found its way here from San Diego & a regular Do#ny Brook fair was in full blast, only the shillelehs were represented by Knives, Lances, Bows & Arrows etc the Gentlemen were rather darker in the complexion & generally sans coullote one Gentleman had his head laid open in the most Scien- : tific manner, at first I thought he had a profusion of . Vermillion plastered over his face & hair but on closer inspection discovered that it was blood all those Indians will tell you that they are American, no Mexi- eanos, they appear particularly eax one to impress on your mind that they have thrown all allSgance to Mexico off with their last old serappa, 15 miles,

quote: by 2 o'clock we entered the rich Vally of Station Maria. herds of Cattle & Horses were quietly pasturing.
full_entry: An early start. led ug over some rough mountain scenery but the day was fine. the Grass Green & the Meadow larks singing all around, it presented more the appearance of an April or May morning than the last of Nov. by 20 clock we entered the rich Vally of Station Maria, herds of Cattle & Horses were quietly pasturing. the only remains of the former Gr&teness of this place is a fine well walled round & the residence of the present proprietor rather a comon adobse House covered in @ great measure with dried Hides, the old Gentleman is very liberal & for a few pieces Tobacco he gave us two fine rounds of Beef newly Killed which proved quite a treat & gave us a few delicious meals, the Indians : carried away the entire offal. not one particle of the animal remaining we camped a short distance from the house, 14 miles.

quote: I ascended one of the mountains & obtained a fine view of the Pacific Ocean, there it lay in quiet Majesty but no Vessels in View.
full_entry: required to Keep one Wagon from oversetting such sidling & precipitous noes I think have rarely been travelled by wheeled Veichls ~ I ascended one of the mountains & obtained a fine’view of the Pacific Ocean, there it lay in quiet Majesty but no Vessels in View. The highest peaks of the Cordelleries were this day passed about 3000 feet above the Ocean & at Evening we camped at the Mission San Diego only some few feet above the sea, vast fields of beautiful Oats lay all along the moun- tains finer than any I had ever seen, better than any cultivated on those our cattle fed with much relish,

quote: this morning I examined the old Mission of San Diego. it is a splendid establishment or has been one as it is now rather falling into ruins.
full_entry: this morning I examined the old Mission of San Diego. it is a splendid establishment or has been one as it is now rather falling into ruins, the principle Building is supported by fifteen square pillars and ranges with the Church which has also three more making a peautiful front. on a fine elevation which overlooks an extensive Garden of some fifteen or twenty acaraXes enclosed with a high Adob&e Wall. two magnificent Palm trees are the first thing which strikes the attention of the traveller, next the great quantity of olive Trees all loaded with the beautiful fruit. hundreds of Bushels hang most temptingly but alas the taste is by no means equal to their appearance. Old Grape Vines are numerous every indication shows that immense labor & expené’e have been bestowed on this extensive Mission, a large Kind of Cactus are planted around the Walls, said to have been fetched from Mexico, Some of the fruit were still on them & I considered them a great delicacy. the Church is in good order & contains many fine paintings and all this splendid place is entirely deserted except when a few emigrants make it a temp@érary home, & their stay by no means help to improve the concern —

quote: we drove down to San Diego distance 6 miles it is a small place, at present garrisoned with a small company of U.S. troops.
today_note: Old Town San Diego State Historic Park preserves the small adobe pueblo Forsyth described as "a small place... a little Adobe Town."
full_entry: we drove down to San Diego distance 6 miles it is a small place,. at present garrisoned with a small company of U. S&S, troops. the temprature of the day was summer & altho a little Adobe Towd every thing looked cheersful, the Mexicans Galloping & officers parading, senorettas with gay dresses ete with the bright sun overhead contributed to make it rather Arrived at the Town of San Diego 3rd Dec, 1849, Day pleasent and warm, Meadow Larks singing and flowers in bloom. The vast and majestic Ocean in quiet repose and 411 nature in one of her most joyous and smiling moods, On the morning of the 4th, however, a change had come over the spirit of the dream -- cold and fitful gusts of wind rushed down from the rugged Gold --~- : Left San Diego 20 December 1849, Arrived : at San Francisco 12 January 1850.
